Conjoined with the Simile of Spraying Foam and Bubbles.
The nature of water is fundamentally without bubbles; when the current is stirred, foam gathers. It assumes various forms and appearances, only to dissolve and return to the void.
The gentleman recognizes the fundamental; why trouble himself with gain and loss? The ignorant masses are startled by transformations, needlessly giving rise to joy and grief.

The nature of flame manifests its characteristics within and without; were it not for the flame, how could one know fire? Moment by moment they shift and pass one another; flickering, they do not remain as they were.
How can those who remain mired in attachment ever understand cause and effect throughout their lives?
The growth of the plantain tree is inherently manifold; its nature is not uniform. It contains buds but does not form seeds; how could its blossoms bear fruit?

The Perfected One excels at employing analogies: when there is no sovereign ruler, who can impose discipline? Do not be intimate with the moment of causal conjunction; you should regard instead the day of dispersal.
Assembled illusions are no different from the craftsman’s artifice—who then would claim they are not real? Once things have passed away, what remains to be recounted?

The deluded doubt whether it is long or short; the enlightened all treat it as their guest. Do not give rise to feelings of separation or union; there has never been a person who lives for a hundred generations.

As one awakens from a dream, one says that while sleeping there was no cognition; yet within the sleep, it was not that nothing was seen. The mental images shine before one’s eyes; likes and dislikes alternate in ten thousand transformations.
Having already realized that the past is but a distant void, I regret my lingering attachment to ephemeral things. Looking closely at this flickering painting, how could it not be of this very land?

Like shadows and echoes responding to forms and sounds, all things depend on external conditions to sustain their existence; yet once they vanish in a sudden flash, by what cause can they be made to resemble their former selves?

Among all beings, there is none that is not thus. In a state of dim obscurity, they call themselves "self. Yet even the four primary colors have no fundamental basis; upon what, then, can the eight subtle elements rely?

Floating clouds overflow, casting shadows over the bright moon; dense mists gather as rain falls from the Southern Mountains. These can produce shifting transformations and functions, yet within me, ultimately nothing is grasped.

In an instant they have already dispersed; how could they ever be gathered back together again? Since all phenomena (*dharma*) are devoid of self (*anātman*), by what means could there be anything belonging to a self (*ātmīya*)?
Like lightning that flashes and strikes with sudden terror—visible yet impossible to pursue—who can analyze the speed or slowness of things once their constant arising and ceasing has passed?

Be careful not to harbor empty attachments; they needlessly cause the divine principle to feel shame. Once [the mind] is aroused, the Way is easily realized; forgetting worldly emotions is a perpetual blessing.
The Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
The Chapter on the Buddha-land.

Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī in the Āmrapālī grove, together with a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus and thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom were renowned and possessed of great wisdom.
He has fully accomplished all fundamental practices. Established by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas, he guards the city of the Dharma and upholds the True Dharma.
He is able to roar the lion’s roar, his fame reaching throughout the ten directions. Without being requested by others, he acts as their friend to bring them peace.
He succeeds and flourishes the Three Jewels, ensuring they are never severed. He subdues demonic adversaries and restrains all those of external paths.

All [faculties] are already purified; forever free from the hindrances and entanglements, their minds always abide in unimpeded liberation, mindfulness, concentration, and dhāraṇī, with eloquence uninterrupted.
In generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and the power of skillful means, there is nothing they do not fully possess.
They have attained the patience of non-arising regarding the non-apprehension of phenomena. Having already been able to...
He turns the irreversible wheel in accordance with the truth; he skillfully understands the characteristics of phenomena and knows the faculties of sentient beings.

He eclipses the great assemblies and attains fearlessness. Having cultivated his mind through merit and wisdom, his body is adorned with the primary and secondary marks, his physical form being foremost among all.
He has renounced all worldly ornaments, yet his fame is so lofty as to surpass Mount Sumeru.
His profound faith is firm and stable, like a vajra. The Jewel of the Dharma shines universally, raining down ambrosia.
Among all vocal expressions, it is the most subtle and supreme. He penetrates deeply into dependent origination and severs all false views regarding the two extremes of existence and non-existence.
He is free from all residual habits. He expounds the Dharma with fearlessness, like the roar of a lion. His preaching resounds like a thunderclap;
it is immeasurable and transcends all measure. Like a guide across the ocean, he gathers the treasures of the many Dharmas.
He thoroughly understands the profound and subtle meanings of all phenomena, and he skillfully knows the destinations of beings' past and future migrations as well as the movements of their minds.
He draws near to the peerless wisdom of the Buddha’s sovereignty, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities.
He closes the gates to all evil destinies and yet manifests his body within the five realms of existence as a great king of physicians.
He is skilled at healing all ailments, providing medicine according to the illness so that it may be taken and practiced.
He has fully accomplished immeasurable merits and purified immeasurable Buddha-lands. Those who see or hear him do not fail to receive benefit;
whatever he does is never in vain. Thus, he is endowed with all such merits in their entirety. His name is...

They were: the Bodhisattva Equal Contemplation, the Bodhisattva Unequal Contemplation, the Bodhisattva Equal and Unequal Contemplation, the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Samādhi, the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Dharma, the Bodhisattva Dharma-Mark, and the Bodhisattva Light-Mark.
The Bodhisattva Prabhāvyūha, the Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha, the Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa, the Bodhisattva Pratibhānakūṭa, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi,
the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāpāṇi, the Bodhisattva Nityotkṣiptahasta, the Bodhisattva Nityanikṣiptahasta, the Bodhisattva Nityodvigna,
the Bodhisattva Priyamūla, the Bodhisattva Priyarāja, the Bodhisattva Pratibhānaghoṣa, and the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja.
The Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva Holding the Precious Torch, the Bodhisattva Jewel Courage, the Bodhisattva Jewel Vision, the Bodhisattva Imperial Net,
the Bodhisattva Luminous Net, the Bodhisattva Objectless Contemplation, the Bodhisattva Accumulated Wisdom, and the Bodhisattva Jewel Victorious.
The Bodhisattva Heavenly King; the Bodhisattva Destroyer of Māra; the Bodhisattva Lightning Virtue; the Bodhisattva Sovereign King;
the Bodhisattva Adorned with Marks of Merit; the Bodhisattva Lion’s Roar; the Bodhisattva Thunder Sound;
the Bodhisattva Mountain-Clashing Sound; the Bodhisattva Fragrant Elephant; the Bodhisattva White Fragrant Elephant; and the Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent, who never rests.
The Bodhisattva Śāntamati, the Bodhisattva Suśruta, the Bodhisattva Avataṃsaka, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Bodhisattva Brahmajāla, the Bodhisattva Ratnadaṇḍa, the Bodhisattva Anabhibhūta, the Bodhisattva Kṣetravyūha,
the Bodhisattva Suvarṇacūḍa, the Bodhisattva Maṇicūḍa, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, and the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī.
The prince-bodhisattvas and thirty-two thousand others such as these, as well as ten thousand Brahma kings including Śikhin and his peers,
came from other four-continent worlds to the place where the Buddha was in order to hear the Dharma. Furthermore,
twelve thousand Śakras also came from other four-continent worlds and took their seats in the assembly, along with other great beings.
The powerful devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and so forth, all came and sat in the assembly.
The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās also all came and sat in the assembly. At that time, the Buddha was with immeasurable hundreds of thousands—
Surrounded by a multitude who paid him respectful homage, he preached the Dharma for them.
Like Sumeru, the king of mountains, appearing majestically above the great ocean, he sat upon a lion throne adorned with various jewels, outshining the entire assembly that had gathered.

At that time, in the city of Vaiśālī, there was the son of an elder named Ratnākara, who, together with five hundred sons of elders, each holding a parasol made of the seven precious gems, came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves at his feet and each offered their own parasol to the Buddha.
Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, all those precious parasols were merged into a single parasol that covered [the entire assembly].
It covered the trichiliocosm, and the broad and long characteristics of this world were all manifested within it.

Furthermore, all the Mount Sumerus, Snow Mountains, Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, Fragrant Mountains, Jewel Mountains, Gold Mountains, Black Mountains, and Iron Mountains of this trichiliocosm...

The surrounding mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains (*Mahācakravāḍa*), the great oceans, rivers, streams, springs, and sources, as well as the sun, moon, and stars, and the palaces of the devas, the palaces of the nāgas, and the palaces of all the honored deities—all appeared within the precious canopy.
Furthermore, the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Buddhas preaching the Dharma also appeared within the precious canopy. At that time, the entire great assembly...

Beholding the Buddha’s supernatural power, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. With palms joined, they prostrated before the Buddha and gazed up at his venerable countenance, their eyes never for a moment wavering.
Then, the elder’s son Ratnākara, standing before the Buddha, spoke in verse:
Your eyes are pure, long, and wide like blue lotuses; your mind is pure, having long transcended all meditative concentrations.
Having accumulated immeasurable pure karma, you lead the multitudes through tranquility;
I bow my head to you, Great Sage, who, having manifested spiritual transformations, universally appears in the infinite lands of the ten directions.
Within them, the Buddhas expound the Dharma; thus all see and hear it.
The Dharma-King’s power of the Dharma transcends all living beings; he constantly bestows the wealth of the Dharma upon all.
He is able to skillfully discern the characteristics of all phenomena, remaining unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Having attained mastery over all phenomena, I therefore bow my head to this King of Dharma.
He teaches that phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent; they arise through causes and conditions.
There is no self, no creator, and no experiencer; yet the karmic fruits of good and evil deeds do not perish.

Originally at the Bodhi tree, you subdued Māra by your power; having attained the realization of the Way of the extinction of ambrosia, you were without mind or intention and without perception or activity, yet you utterly defeated all non-Buddhists.
You turned the Wheel of Dharma thrice throughout the great trichiliocosm; that wheel is from the beginning eternally pure.
Devas and humans who have attained the Way take this as their witness; thus the Three Jewels appear in the world.
By means of this wondrous Dharma, you deliver all living beings; once received, they do not regress and remain eternally tranquil.
O Great King of Physicians, who delivers them from old age, sickness, death, and birth—homage should be paid to the Dharma Ocean of boundless virtue.
Unshaken by praise or blame, like Mount Sumeru; regarding the good and the bad with equal compassion, you act with equanimity like space.
Who, upon hearing of this Human Jewel, would not receive him with reverence?
Now I offer this humble canopy to the World-Honored One, within which the three thousandfold world-system appears.
The palaces where the devas, nāgas, and spirits dwell, and those of the gandharvas and yakṣas—all that exists in the world—is seen;
out of compassion, the One of Ten Powers has manifested this miraculous transformation.
Beholding this rarity, the multitudes all praise the Buddha: "Now I bow my head to the Honored One of the Three Realms."
The Great Sage, Dharma King, to whom all turn in homage— Those with pure hearts who contemplate the Buddha find nothing but joy.
Each beholds the World-Honored One standing before them; This is the unique power of his spiritual authority.
When the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, Sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind.
All say that the World-Honored One speaks in accordance with their own language; this is a supernatural power, a unique quality not shared [by others].
When the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings each understand it according to their own capacity;
they all receive and practice it, thereby obtaining its benefit. This is a supernatural power, a unique quality not shared [by others].
The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice; some feel fear, some rejoice, some develop weary detachment, and some sever their doubts. This is the unshared power of his spiritual authority.
I bow my head to the One of Ten Powers, the Greatly Diligent; I bow my head to the One who has attained the Fearlessnesses.
I prostrate to you who abide in the unique qualities; I prostrate to all you great guides.
I prostrate to you who can sever all fetters and bonds; I prostrate to you who have reached the further shore.
I prostrate to you who can deliver all the worlds; I prostrate to you who are forever free from the path of birth and death.
Fully knowing the marks of the coming and going of sentient beings, Skillful in all dharmas, you have attained liberation;
Unattached to the world like a lotus flower, You always skillfully enter the practice of emptiness and stillness.
Reaching the true nature of all dharmas without hindrance, I prostrate to you who are like space, having no dependence.
At that time, after the elder’s son Ratnākara had spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, these five hundred sons of elders have all already resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
They wish to hear about attaining the purity of a buddha-field. We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the pure lands of the bodhisattvas."
[The assembly] practiced. The Buddha said, "Excellent, Ratnākara! You have been able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the practice for the pure land of all bodhisattvas.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for you.
Thereupon, Ratnākara and five hundred sons of elders received the instruction and listened. The Buddha said, "Ratnākara, as for sentient beings—"
Such is the buddha-field of a bodhisattva. Why is this? A bodhisattva takes up a buddha-field according to the beings they transform;
they take up a buddha-field according to the beings they discipline; they take up a buddha-field according to whatever realm is appropriate for sentient beings to enter the wisdom of a Buddha;
and they take up a buddha-field according to whatever [is appropriate] for sentient beings...

The Land. One arouses the roots of a bodhisattva and thereby takes up a buddha-field. Why is this? It is because when a bodhisattva takes up a pure land, it is entirely for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
For example, suppose there is a person who wishes to construct a palace on a vacant plot of ground;
they can do so as they please without hindrance. However, if they attempt to build it in empty space, it can never be accomplished. A bodhisattva is like this...
It is so. For the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity, one vows to take up a Buddha-field. To vow to take up a Buddha-field is not to do so in emptiness alone.
Ratnākara, you should know that a straightforward mind is the pure land of a bodhisattva. When the bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, [the beings of that land will likewise be straightforward].
Not being sycophantic toward sentient beings is a pure land of the bodhisattva; when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who possess deep resolve will be born in that land.
Deep resolve is a pure land of the bodhisattva; when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings endowed with merit will be born in that land.
The bodhicitta is a pure land of the bodhisattva; when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings of the Mahāyāna will be born in that land. Generosity is...
The pure land of a bodhisattva: when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, all sentient beings capable of renunciation will come to be born in that land.

Precept-keeping is the pure land of a bodhisattva: when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who practice the ten paths of wholesome action and fulfill their vows will come to be born in that land. Patience is the pure land of a bodhisattva: when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood...
At that time, sentient beings adorned with the thirty-two marks will come to be born in that land. Diligence is the pure land of a bodhisattva;
when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who diligently cultivate all merits will come to be born in that land.
Meditative concentration is the pure land of a bodhisattva; when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, those who have gathered their minds and are undisturbed...
Birth: When a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who possess right concentration will come to be born in that land. Wisdom is the pure land of a Bodhisattva;
when a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who possess right concentration will come to be born in that land. The four immeasurable minds are the pure land of a Bodhisattva;

when a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who have accomplished loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity will come to be born in that land. The four methods of attraction...
This is the pure land of that bodhisattva. When that bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who have been gathered through liberation will come to be born in that land.

Skillful means (*upāya*) is the pure land of that bodhisattva. When that bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who possess unimpeded skillful means regarding all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) will come to be born in that land.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are the pure land of that bodhisattva... [and so forth].

The Pure Land: when a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who practice the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path will be reborn in that land.
The mind of dedication is the pure land of this Bodhisattva; when this Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, [those with such a mind will be reborn there].
To attain a land of sovereign excellence endowed with all perfections is to speak of the removal of the eight difficulties; this is the pure land of a bodhisattva.
When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, there shall be no three evil realms or eight difficulties in that land.

To maintain one’s own observance of the precepts without mocking the deficiencies of others is the pure land of a bodhisattva. When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, there shall be no transgressions in that land.

The names of the prohibitions are the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala*). These constitute the pure land of the bodhisattva. When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings will not suffer premature death;
they will possess great wealth and practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*); their speech will be truthful and always gentle; their retinues will never be separated from them;

they will skillfully harmonize disputes and litigation; their words will invariably be beneficial; and they will be free from envy and anger. Sentient beings with right view will be reborn in that land.
“Country. Thus, Ratnākara, as a bodhisattva follows his straightforward mind, he is able to initiate practice;
as he follows his initiation of practice, he attains the profound mind; as he follows his profound mind, his will becomes subdued; as his will is subdued, he acts according to what he has said;
as he acts according to what he has said, he is able to perform dedication; as he performs dedication, he possesses the proper method.”
According to one's skillful means, one brings sentient beings to maturity; according to the maturation of sentient beings, the Buddha-field becomes pure;
according to the purity of the Buddha-field, the teaching of the Dharma becomes pure; according to the purity of the teaching of the Dharma, wisdom becomes pure;
according to the purity of wisdom, the mind becomes pure; according to the purity of the mind, all merits become pure. This is...
"Therefore, Ratnākara, if a bodhisattva wishes to attain a pure land, they should purify their own mind. To the extent that the mind is purified, the buddha-field is purified.
At that time, Śāriputra, sustained by the Buddha's majestic spiritual power, had this thought: "If the bodhisattva’s mind is pure, then..."
“Regarding the purity of the Buddha-field: O World-Honored One, when you were formerly a bodhisattva, was your mind not pure?
And yet, this Buddha-field is so impure. The Buddha, knowing his thought, immediately addressed him, saying: “What do you think?”
"Are the sun and moon not pure? Yet the blind do not see them. He replied, "No, World-Honored One;
it is the fault of the blind, not the fault of the sun and moon. "Śāriputra, it is because of the transgressions of sentient beings that they do not see the majestic purity of the Tathāgata’s land;
it is not the fault of the Tathāgata. Śāriputra, this land of mine is pure, yet you do not perceive it."
[He] saw it. At that time, the Brahmā Śikhin said to Śāriputra, "Do not harbor such a thought as to say that this buddha-field is impure.
Why is this? I see the buddha-field of Śākyamuni Buddha as pure, like the palace of the Lord of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Śāriputra said, "As for me, I see this land with its hills, mounds, and ravines..."
Khan. Thorns, brambles, gravel, sand, and mountains of earth and stone—filled with all manner of filth and impurity.
The Brahma King Śikhin said, "Virtuous one, it is because your mind harbors high and low and does not rely on the Buddha’s wisdom that you perceive this land as impure."
"Śāriputra, bodhisattvas are entirely equal toward all sentient beings;
with a deeply pure mind and relying on the wisdom of the Buddha, they are able to see this buddha-field as pure.
Thereupon, the Buddha pressed the earth with his toe, and immediately the trichiliocosm was adorned with hundreds of thousands of various precious jewels.

It was as if the land of the Buddha Ratnavyūha, adorned with the jewels of immeasurable merit, were being praised by the entire great assembly as something unprecedented, and they all saw themselves sitting upon jeweled lotus flowers.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra, "Observe, for a moment, the purity and adornment of this buddha-field. Śāriputra replied, "Indeed, World-Honored One; it is such as I have never before seen."
[He] saw what he had never heard before: the Buddha-land was now entirely manifest as adorned and pure. The Buddha told Śāriputra, "My Buddha-land is always pure like this.
It is because I wish to deliver those of inferior capacity that I manifest this land of manifold evils and impurity.
It is, for example, like the gods who eat from a common precious vessel; according to their respective merits, [the food appears differently to each]."
The color of the rice was different. It is even so, Śāriputra. If a person’s mind is pure, they will see this land adorned with its merits.

When the Buddha manifested the purity and adornment of this land, the five hundred sons of elders led by Ratnākara all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). Eighty-four thousand people all resolved their minds upon [enlightenment].
[The Buddha] restored the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The Buddha withdrew his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), and this world returned to its former state.

Thirty-two thousand gods and humans who sought the vehicle of the śrāvaka, realizing that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are entirely impermanent, became free from dust and defilement and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣur-viśuddhi*). Eight thousand bhikṣus... [did not...]
Experiencing all dharmas, his outflows were exhausted and his mind was liberated.
From the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Volume Two,
Chapter on Expedient Means.
At that time, in the great city of Vaiśālī, there was an elder named Vimalakīrti.
He had already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in the past, deeply planted the roots of goodness, attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*),
possessed unimpeded eloquence, sported with supernatural powers, mastered all *dhāraṇīs*, obtained fearlessness, subdued Māras and their enmities, and entered into the profound Dharma.
He was proficient in the *Prajñāpāramitā* and thoroughly mastered skillful means (*upāya*). His great vows were fulfilled, and he clearly understood the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings.
Furthermore, he could discern the sharpness or dullness of their faculties. Having long practiced the Buddha-way, his mind was already pure and mature; he was firmly resolved upon the Mahāyāna.
In all that he did, he was able to deliberate with wisdom, abiding in the majestic deportment of a Buddha. His mind...

Vast as the ocean, praised by all Buddhas, and revered by his disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, and the lords of the world, he dwells in Vaiśālī through skillful means for the sake of delivering sentient beings. Possessing immeasurable wealth, he gathers in the poor;
upholding the precepts with purity, he gathers in those who violate them; through the practice of patience, he gathers in those who are wrathful; and with great vigor...
He advances to gather in all who are indolent; with single-minded meditative stillness, he gathers in all whose minds are distracted; and with resolute wisdom, he gathers in all who lack knowledge.
Although he is a layman, he upholds the pure disciplinary conduct of a śramaṇa; although he dwells at home, he is not attached to the triple world.
He manifests having a wife and children, yet he constantly cultivates the brahma-conduct; he appears to have kinsmen, yet he is always...
He delights in seclusion. Though he wears precious ornaments, he adorns his body with the marks and signs of excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
Though he partakes of food and drink, he takes the joy of meditation (*dhyāna-prīti*) as his true flavor. When he arrives at places of gambling and games, he immediately uses them to deliver others.

Among followers of various heterodox paths, he does not disparage their correct faith. Though he is well-versed in worldly classics, he always delights in the Buddha-dharma. Thus, he is honored and respected by all.
He is the most supreme among those who make offerings. He upholds the True Dharma and gathers together both the elderly and the young.
All his worldly affairs are harmonious and successful; yet though he obtains secular profit, he does not take delight in it. He frequents the four crossroads to benefit sentient beings.

He enters places where the True Dharma is administered to rescue and protect all. He enters places of debate and instruction to guide others by means of the Mahāyāna. He enters various schools of learning.
He entices the ignorant and leads them into brothels to demonstrate the faults of desire; he enters wine shops to enable them to establish their resolve.
If he is among elders, he is honored as the most venerable among them and preaches the supreme Dharma; if he is among householders...
Among householders, he is the most honored; he cuts off their greedy attachments. If among kṣatriyas, he is the most honored among kṣatriyas; he teaches them patience.
If among brahmins, he is the most honored among brahmins; he removes their pride.
If among ministers, he is the most honored among ministers; he teaches them the True Dharma. If among princes, he is the most honored among princes.
He demonstrates loyalty and filial piety; if he is among the inner court officials, he is the most honored among them, transforming and correcting the palace women.
If he is among the common people, he is the most honored among them, causing the power of merit to arise. If he is among the Brahmā devas, he is the most honored among them.
He instructs them with supreme wisdom. If he is among the Śakras, he is the most honored among the Śakras, manifesting impermanence.
If he is among the World-Protectors (Lokapālas), he is the most honored among the World-Protectors, protecting all sentient beings.

In this way, the Elder Vimalakīrti benefits sentient beings through such immeasurable skillful means. By means of these expedients, he manifests himself as being ill (his past and present ailments are connected through the continuity of his vital energies).
Because of his illness, kings, ministers, elders, householders, brahmins, as well as princes and other officials—countless thousands in all—went to inquire after his health.
To those who came, Vimalakīrti, on account of his physical ailment, extensively expounded the Dharma, saying: "O noble ones, this body is impermanent and lacks strength."
It is powerless, lacking solidity, and subject to rapid decay; it is not to be trusted. It is suffering and affliction, a gathering place for manifold diseases.
O worthy ones, such a body as this is not to be relied upon by the wise. This body is like a mass of foam, incapable of being grasped or touched.
This body is like a bubble, unable to endure for long. This body is like a flame... from... [it arises].
Thirst arises. This body is like a plantain tree; it has no solidity within. This body is like an illusion, arising from inversion.
This body is like a dream, consisting of false perceptions. This body is like a shadow, appearing through the conditions of karma.
This body is like an echo, dependent upon various causes and conditions. This body is like a floating cloud, changing and perishing in an instant.
This body is like lightning, not remaining for even a single thought-moment. This body has no master, being like the earth.
This body has no self, being like fire. This body has no life-span, being like wind. This body has no person, being like water. This...
The body is not substantial; the four great elements constitute its abode. This body is empty, devoid of self and what belongs to self.
This body is insentient, like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles. This body is inactive, driven by the power of the winds. This body is impure.
It is filled with filth and impurity. This body is deceptive; though it is provisionally sustained by bathing, clothing, and food, it must inevitably return to decay and extinction.
This body is a calamity, afflicted by one hundred and one maladies. This body is like a dilapidated well, pressed down by old age.
This body is unstable, for it is destined to die. This body is like a venomous serpent, like a hostile thief, like...

It is like an empty village, composed of the common aggregation of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas). O worthy ones, this is something to be weary of and loathe;
you should instead take delight in the Buddha-body. Why is this? The Buddha-body is the Dharma-body. It is born from immeasurable merit and wisdom;
it is born from morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; it is born from loving-kindness and compassion.

It is born from joyful relinquishment; it is born from generosity, ethical discipline, patience, gentleness, diligent application, vigor, meditative concentration, liberation, samādhi, extensive learning, and wisdom—the various pāramitās (which mean "reaching the other shore"); it is born from skillful means; it is born from the six supernormal powers;
it is born from the three types of clear knowledge; it is born from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; and it is born from tranquility and insight.
It arises from the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
It arises from the abandonment of all unwholesome dharmas and the accumulation of all wholesome dharmas. It arises from reality; it arises from heedfulness.
The body of a Tathāgata arises from such immeasurable pure dharmas. O worthy ones, if you wish to attain the body of a Buddha, [you must cultivate these].
"Those who wish to sever all the illnesses of sentient beings should resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Thus, the Elder Vimalakīrti, for the sake of those who had come to inquire after his illness, preached the Dharma as was appropriate,
causing countless thousands of people to all resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
The Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Three:
Chapter on the Disciples.
At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti thought to himself as he lay ill upon his bed: "The World-Honored One is greatly compassionate; would it not be fitting..."
The Buddha did not show compassion [by sending him]. Knowing his thoughts, the Buddha immediately addressed Śāriputra:
"Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness. Śāriputra said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness."
Why is this? I recall that in the past, while I was sitting in meditative seclusion beneath a tree in a grove, Vimalakīrti came to me and said:
"Śāriputra, it is not necessarily by sitting in this manner that one practices meditative seclusion."
Now, as for "sitting in meditation": not manifesting body or mind within the three realms—this is sitting in meditation.
Not arising from the samādhi of cessation while manifesting various modes of deportment—this is sitting in meditation.

Not abandoning the dharmas of the Path while manifesting the affairs of ordinary people—this is sitting in meditation. When the mind dwells neither within nor without—this is sitting in meditation. Regarding...
To practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment without being moved by any views—this is true sitting in meditation.
To enter nirvana without severing the afflictions—this is true sitting in meditation. If one can sit in such a manner, it is approved by the Buddha.
At that time, World-Honored One, having heard these words, I remained silent and ceased speaking, unable to offer a further reply. Therefore...
"I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
The Buddha said to Mahāmaudgalyāyana, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire about his illness.
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not capable of going to him to inquire about his illness. Why is this? I recall..."
Once, when I had entered the great city of Vaiśālī and was preaching the Dharma to the lay devotees in the midst of the streets and alleys, Vimalakīrti came to me and said:
"O Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you preach the Dharma to lay devotees who are householders."
It should not be as the benevolent one has described. Now, one who preaches the Dharma should preach it according to the Dharma.
The Dharma has no sentient beings, because it is free from the defilement of sentient beings. The Dharma has no self, because it is free from the defilement of the self. The Dharma has no life-span.
Because it is free from birth and death, dharmas have no person. Because the prior and posterior limits are severed, dharmas are eternally quiescent.
Because all marks are extinguished, dharmas are free from marks. Because there is nothing to be perceived, dharmas are without names. Because speech is severed, dharmas cannot be spoken.
Because they are free from applied and sustained thought, dharmas have no form or appearance; they are like empty space. Thus are dharmas.
There is no conceptual proliferation, because it is ultimately empty. Phenomena have no "mine," because they are free from the notion of "mine.
Phenomena have no discrimination, because they are free from all consciousnesses. Phenomena have no counterpart, because they do not depend on anything else.

Phenomena do not belong to causes, because they do not abide in conditions. Phenomena are identical with the dharma-nature, because they enter into all phenomena. Phenomena accord with suchness, yet there is nothing to which they accord.
Therefore, phenomena abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), for they do not move toward any extremes. Phenomena are without fluctuation, for they do not rely upon the six sense objects.
Phenomena have no coming or going, for they never abide. Phenomena accord with emptiness, follow signlessness, and correspond to wishlessness.
The Dharma is free from the beautiful and the ugly. The Dharma has no increase or decrease. The Dharma has no arising or ceasing. The Dharma has no place of return.
The Dharma transcends the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind. The Dharma has no high or low. The Dharma is eternally abiding and immovable.
The Dharma is free from all modes of contemplative practice. O Mahāmaudgalyāyana, such is the nature of the Dharma; how can it be described? Indeed, as for preaching the Dharma—
There is neither speaking nor demonstrating; those who hear the Dharma neither hear nor attain it. It is like a phantom person preaching the Dharma for a phantom person.

One should establish this intention when preaching the Dharma, clearly discerning that the faculties of sentient beings are either sharp or dull, being skillful in knowledge and vision without any obstruction. With a mind of great compassion, one should praise the Mahāyāna.
"Only after contemplating how to repay the Buddha’s kindness and ensuring that the Three Jewels are not interrupted shall I preach the Dharma.
When Vimalakīrti spoke these words, eight hundred lay devotees resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
I lack such eloquence; therefore, I am unfit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
The Buddha said to Mahākāśyapa, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness. Why is this?
I recall that in the past, while I was begging for alms in a poor neighborhood, Vimalakīrti came and said to me: 'O Mahākāśyapa!'"
One possesses a heart of compassion, yet it cannot be universal. One abandons the wealthy and noble to beg from the poor.
Kāśyapa, you should dwell in the dharma of equality and go on alms-round in regular order. You should go on alms-round for the sake of non-eating.
You should take morsel-food for the sake of destroying the perception of combination. You should accept that food for the sake of non-acceptance. By means of the "empty village" [meditation]...

(One should maintain this mental state whenever entering a village. Upon entering a village: regard all forms seen as equal to those of a blind person; regard all sounds heard as equal to echoes; regard all odors smelled as equal to the wind;
do not discriminate among the flavors tasted; experience all tactile sensations as if through direct realization;
and know all phenomena to be like illusions—devoid of intrinsic nature and devoid of extrinsic nature, fundamentally non-arising from the beginning, and now likewise non-existent.
"Extinction. Kāśyapa, if you can enter the eight liberations without abandoning the eight wrong paths; if you can enter the true Dharma by means of the characteristics of the wrong;
if you can give a single meal to all beings, thereby making offerings to all Buddhas and the assembly of worthy sages—only then may you eat.
One who eats in this manner has neither afflictions nor is free from afflictions; they have neither entered a state of meditative concentration nor..."
Arising from meditative concentration, he dwells neither in the world nor in nirvana. For one who gives to such a person, there is no great merit and no small merit;
it is neither for benefit nor for harm. This is the correct entry into the Buddha-way, not relying on the śrāvakas.

Kāśyapa, if one eats in this manner, one does not eat the alms of others in vain. At that time, I— *Note: The final phrase "At that time, I—" appears to be an incomplete fragment of the original text.*
When the Venerable One heard these words, he attained what he had never experienced before.
He immediately conceived a profound sense of reverence toward all bodhisattvas and further thought: "One who possesses such a noble name, eloquence, and wisdom as this can indeed speak thus.
Who would not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? From this point forward, I shall no longer..."
Furthermore, he exhorted others toward the practices of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. For this reason, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
The Buddha said to Subhūti, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire about his illness.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness. Why is this? As I recall—"
Formerly, when I entered his house to beg for alms, Vimalakīrti took my bowl and filled it with food, saying to me:
"O Subhūti, if you can regard food as equal, then all dharmas are also equal;
if all dharmas are equal, then food is also equal. Only by begging in this manner may you take this food. If, Subhūti..."
He does not sever lust, anger, and delusion, yet he does not dwell with them. He does not destroy the body, yet he accords with the single mark.

He does not extinguish ignorance and craving, yet he gives rise to clarity and liberation. He attains liberation through the characteristics of the five heinous crimes. He is neither liberated nor bound;
he does not perceive the Four Truths, yet it is not that he does not perceive the Truths; he has not attained the fruits [of the path], yet it is not that he has not attained the fruits. It is not...
An ordinary person is not apart from the dharmas of an ordinary person; they are not a noble one, nor are they not a noble one.
Although they are accomplished in all dharmas, they are detached from the characteristics of all dharmas; only then may they accept the food. Subhūti, if you do not perceive a Buddha...

"You have not heard the Dharma. Those six heterodox teachers—Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarin Gośālīputra, Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra—are your teachers. Because of this...
"Since he has gone forth [into homelessness], wherever that teacher falls, you too shall fall. Only then may you take this food.

Subhūti, if you enter into various false views, fail to reach the further shore, dwell among the eight difficulties and fail to attain freedom from difficulty, and become identical with afflictions while remaining apart from the pure Dharma—then all sentient beings shall likewise attain the Samādhi of Non-contention."
Having attained this samādhi, those who give to you cannot be called fields of merit; those who make offerings to you will fall into the three evil realms.
You act with one hand in league with the various māras, serving as their companions in toil.
You are no different from the various māras and the afflictions (*kleśa*). Toward all sentient beings, you harbor a heart of enmity, and you slander the Buddhas.
"They have subverted the Dharma; they do not enter the ranks of the assembly and shall never attain parinirvāṇa.
If you are such as this, then you may take this food. At that time, our World-Honored One heard these words and was bewildered;
he did not know what they meant and did not know how to respond. He set down his bowl and wished to leave the house. Vimalakīrti said, "Subhūti, take it!"
“Bhadrapāla, do not be afraid. What do you think? If a person created as a magical emanation by the Tathāgata were to be questioned on this matter, would they feel any fear?
I replied, “No. Vimalakīrti said, “All dharmas have the nature of a magical illusion; you should not feel any fear. Why is this? All verbal expressions...”
One does not depart from these marks. As for the wise, they do not cling to words; therefore, they have nothing to fear.
Why is this? The nature of words is detached; there are no words, and this is liberation. That which is the mark of liberation is precisely all phenomena (*dharmas*).
When Vimalakīrti spoke this Dharma, two hundred devaputras attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
"Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness.
The Buddha said to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not capable of going to him to inquire after his illness. Why is this?"
Why is this? I recall that in the past, while I was in a great forest sitting beneath a tree preaching the Dharma to newly ordained bhikṣus, Vimalakīrti came and said to me:
"Pūrṇa, you should first enter meditative concentration and observe the minds of these people before preaching the Dharma. Do not place foul food into a precious vessel."
You should know the thoughts in this bhikṣu’s mind. Do not equate lapis lazuli with crystal.
You do not understand the fundamental dispositions of sentient beings; do not attempt to inspire them by means of the Hīnayāna vehicle.
They have no wounds themselves, so do not injure them. Those who wish to travel the Great Road must not be shown a narrow path. Do not try to contain the great ocean within...
Within a cow’s footprint, one cannot equate the sunlight with the glow of a firefly.
Pūrṇa, this bhikṣu long ago gave rise to the mind of the Mahāyāna, though he has temporarily forgotten that intention; how can you instruct him with the teachings of the Hīnayāna?
I observe that the wisdom of the Śrāvakas is slight and shallow, like that of a blind person; they are unable to distinguish the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of all sentient beings.

At that moment, Vimalakīrti entered into samādhi and caused these bhikṣus to recognize their own past lives, seeing that they had planted the roots of various virtues under five hundred buddhas and dedicated them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
They attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. At that moment, their minds were suddenly opened wide, and they recovered their original state of mind.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus bowed their heads at the feet of Vimalakīrti.
Then Vimalakīrti preached the Dharma for them, so that they never again regressed from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. I reflect upon the śrāvakas...
"One should not preach the Dharma without observing the faculties of others; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
The Buddha said to Mahākātyāyana, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire about his illness.
Kātyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness. Why is this? I recall—"
I recall that in the past, the Buddha briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the bhikṣus.
Immediately thereafter, I elaborated upon their meaning—namely, the meaning of impermanence, the meaning of suffering, the meaning of emptiness, the meaning of non-self, and the meaning of cessation.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me: "Kātyāyana, do not use a mind characterized by arising and ceasing to speak of reality."
Regarding the nature of phenomena, Kātyāyana: that all phenomena are ultimately neither born nor extinguished is the meaning of impermanence.
That the five aggregates of clinging are thoroughly penetrated as empty and without arising is the meaning of suffering. That all phenomena are ultimately non-existent is the meaning of selflessness.
This is the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*): that "self" and "non-self" are non-dual; this is the meaning of non-self (*anātman*).

That dharmas were originally not ignited and are now not extinguished—this is the meaning of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*). When he spoke these dharmas, those bhikṣus attained liberation of mind.
Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness.
The Buddha said to Aniruddha, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Aniruddha addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness. Why is this?
I recall that once, while I was walking in meditation at a certain place, there was a Brahmā king named Śuddhavimāna who came with ten thousand Brahmās."
Emitting pure radiance, he came to where I was, prostrated himself in salutation, and asked me:
"To what extent, Ānanda, does the divine eye perceive? I immediately replied:

"O worthy one, I see this Sahā world-system of Śākyamuni Buddha, a trichiliocosm, as clearly as one would look at an *āmala* fruit (shaped like a *pūga* nut) held in the palm of one's hand. At that time...
Vimalakīrti came and said to me, "O Aniruddha, is that which is seen by your divine eye characterized by conditioned activity (*saṃskṛta*) or is it unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
If it were characterized by conditioned activity, it would be equal to the five supernormal powers of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
If it were unconditioned, it would be the unmanifest (*asaṃskṛta*), and thus there should be no seeing. World-Honored One, at that time I remained silent. Those [monks]...
When Brahmā heard these words, he experienced what he had never before encountered. He immediately prostrated himself in homage and asked, "In the world, who possesses the true divine eye?
Vimalakīrti replied, "There is the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who has attained the true divine eye.
He constantly abides in samādhi and beholds all buddha-fields without perceiving them through dualistic characteristics. Thereupon, the Brahmā King Śuddhāvāsa and...
His retinue of five hundred Brahmās all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having prostrated at the feet of Vimalakīrti, they suddenly vanished. Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness.
The Buddha said to Upāli, “Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Upāli replied to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness. Why is this?
I recall that in the past there were two bhikṣus who had violated the disciplinary rules and felt ashamed of their conduct; they did not dare to ask the Buddha, so they came to question me.”
He said, "O Upāli, we have indeed violated the Vinaya and are truly ashamed; we did not dare to ask the Buddha.
We pray that you will resolve our doubts and regrets so that we may be freed from this fault. I then explained the Dharma for them according to the rules.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me, "O Upāli, do not further increase the offenses of these two bhikṣus. You should..."
Directly eliminate them; do not disturb the mind. Why is this? That nature of sin does not exist within, nor does it exist without, nor does it exist in between.
As the Buddha has said: "Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure.
Furthermore, the mind does not exist within, nor does it exist without, nor does it exist in between. Just as...
"The mind is thus; the defilements of sin are thus; all phenomena are thus; they do not transcend suchness (*tathatā*).
Upāli, when one attains liberation through the characteristic of the mind, is there any defilement at all? I replied, "No.
Vimalakīrti said, "The characteristic of the minds of all sentient beings is likewise free from defilement. It is only, Upāli, due to delusion..."
Conceptualization is defilement; the absence of conceptualization is purity. Inversion is defilement; freedom from inversion is purity.
Grasping at a self is defilement; not grasping at a self is purity. Upāli, all phenomena arise and perish without remaining.
Like illusions and like lightning, all phenomena do not depend upon one another; they do not abide for even a single thought-moment.
All phenomena are false perceptions, like dreams, like mirages, like the moon reflected in water, and like images in a mirror—they arise from deluded conceptualization.
"One who knows this is called one who upholds the Vinaya; one who knows this is called one who has excellent understanding.
Then those two bhikṣus said, "How profound is his wisdom! This is beyond the reach of Upāli; though he is supreme among those who uphold the Vinaya, he cannot explain it.
I replied to them, "Setting aside the Tathāgata himself, there has never been a śrāvaka or a bodhisattva [who could do so]..."
“Sā. He was able to restrain their eloquence in debate; such was the clarity and penetration of his wisdom.
At that time, the doubts and regrets of the two bhikṣus were immediately dispelled, and they resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
He made this vow, saying: "May all sentient beings attain such eloquence as this. Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
The Buddha said to Rāhula, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire about his illness. Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
He said to the World-Honored One, "I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness. Why is this?
I recall that in the past, the sons of the elders of Vaiśālī came to where I was, prostrated themselves in salutation, and asked me:
'O Rāhula, you are the son of the Buddha; you have renounced the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch to leave the household life and pursue the Way.'"
"What are the benefits of going forth? I then explained to him, in accordance with the Dharma, the merits and benefits of renouncing the household life.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me, "Rāhula, you should not speak of the merits and benefits of going forth.
Why is this? To be without benefit and without merit—this is what constitutes going forth."
Conditioned phenomena can be said to possess benefit and merit. But for one who has gone forth, there is unconditioned phenomena;
within unconditioned phenomena, there is neither benefit nor merit. Rāhula, for one who has gone forth, there is neither "that" nor "this," nor anything in between.
Free from the sixty-two views, they abide in nirvāṇa. This is the wise one.
That which is received; the sphere of the noble ones; subduing all Māras; crossing over the five destinies; purifying the five eyes; attaining the five powers;
establishing the five faculties; not afflicting others; being free from all various evils; crushing all non-Buddhists;
transcending provisional names and emerging from the mud; being without attachment, without "mine-ness," without that which is received, and without disturbance within.

"Maintaining joy (with the Way and Dharma filling the interior), protecting the minds of others (encouraging and following sentient beings), conforming to meditative concentration, and remaining free from all faults—if one can act thus, this is true renunciation.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti said to the sons of the elders, "You all should likewise go forth together within the True Dharma.
Why is this? Because a Buddha’s appearance in the world is difficult to encounter. The sons of the elders replied, "Householder..."
I heard the Buddha’s words: "If one's parents do not give permission, one cannot leave the household life. Vimalakīrti said, "That is so.
However, if you all resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, that itself is leaving the household life;
that itself is full ordination. At that time, the thirty-two sons of the elders all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"...the mind of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. Therefore, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am unable to go there to inquire after his illness. Why is this? I recall a time in the past..."
"The Venerable One’s body is slightly unwell and requires cow’s milk. I have therefore taken my bowl and come to stand at the gate of a great brāhmaṇa’s house.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me, "Ānanda, why do you stand here with your bowl so early in the morning?
I replied, "Householder, the World-Honored One’s body is slightly unwell and requires cow’s milk..."
"...milk. Therefore, I have come here. Vimalakīrti said, "Stop, stop, Ānanda! Do not speak such words.
The body of the Tathāgata is a diamond-like essence; all evils have been severed, and all virtues are universally assembled.
How could there be any illness? How could there be any affliction? Be silent and depart, Ānanda! Do not slander the Tathāgata, lest others hear it."
Do not let these coarse words be heard by the gods of great majesty and power, nor by the bodhisattvas who have come from the pure lands of other directions.
Ānanda, even a wheel-turning sage king, owing to his meager merit, still attains freedom from illness;
how much more so the Tathāgata, who possesses immeasurable accumulations of merit and is universally supreme? Depart, Ānanda! Do not [speak thus].
It brings such shame upon us that if non-Buddhist brahmins were to hear these words, they would think:
"What kind of teacher is this? Unable to save himself from his own illness, how can he claim to save those who are ill?
You must depart quickly and in secret so that no one hears this. Ānanda, you should know that the bodies of all Tathāgatas are, in truth, the Dharma-body.
The Buddha is not a body of thought or desire; he is the World-Honored One who has transcended the three realms. The Buddha’s body is without outflows (*anāsrava*); all outflows have been exhausted.
The Buddha’s body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall within the realm of numerical categories. For such a body as this, how could there be any illness?
At that time, O World-Honored One, I was truly filled with shame and remorse, wondering if I had approached the Buddha and misunderstood what was heard.
Immediately, I heard a voice from the air saying: "Ānanda, it is as the householder says; it is only because the Buddha has appeared in this world of five turbidities."
"He manifests this Dharma to deliver sentient beings. Go, Ānanda; take the milk without shame.
"World-Honored One, such are the wisdom and eloquence of Vimalakīrti. Therefore, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.
Thus did each of the five hundred great disciples individually relate their own past circumstances to the Buddha, recounting them as follows.
Vimalakīrti said to them all, "None of you are fit to go there to inquire after his illness.
This concludes the fourth chapter, "The Bodhisattvas," from the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra.
Thereupon the Buddha said to Maitreya Bodhisattva, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness. Why is this?
I recall that in the past, when I was the King of Tuṣita Heaven, I was preaching the stage of non-retrogression for him and his retinue."
[This was] the practice (namely, the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas). At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me:

"Maitreya, the World-Honored One has bestowed upon you the prediction that in one more birth you shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (Unsurpassed, Perfect, and Complete Enlightenment). By which birth do you receive this prediction?
Is it by a past birth, a future birth, or a present birth? If it is by a past birth, [then] a past birth..."
That which has already ceased has perished. If it were to arise in the future, the future arising has not yet arrived.
If it were to arise in the present, the present arising has no duration. As the Buddha said: "O bhikṣu, at this very moment you are simultaneously being born, aging, and ceasing."
If one receives a prediction of enlightenment through non-arising, then non-arising is itself the state of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
Within that state of true reality, there is neither receiving a prediction nor attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
How then, Maitreya, can you receive the prediction of being born only once more? Is it from the arising of suchness (*tathatā*) that one receives the prediction, or from suchness itself?
Is one granted the prediction of enlightenment through the extinction of suchness? If one were granted the prediction through the arising of suchness, suchness has no arising.
If one were granted the prediction through the extinction of suchness, suchness has no extinction. All sentient beings are suchness.
All dharmas are also suchness; all sages and worthies are also suchness; even unto Maitreya, he is also suchness.
If Maitreya is to receive the prediction of enlightenment, then all sentient beings should also receive the prediction.
Why is this? For suchness is neither dual nor different. If Maitreya attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*...
As for Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, all sentient beings should likewise attain it. Why is this?
Because all sentient beings are themselves the very mark of bodhi. If Maitreya attains parinirvāṇa, then all sentient beings shall also attain parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because the Buddhas know that all sentient beings are ultimately quiescent.
Cessation is itself the characteristic of *nirvāṇa*; it does not cease further. Therefore, Maitreya, do not attempt to entice these sons of the gods with this teaching.
In truth, there is no one who gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor is there anyone who regresses from it.
Maitreya, you should cause these sons of the gods to abandon their conceptualization of bodhi.
[He] saw. Why was this? Enlightenment cannot be attained by means of the body, nor can it be attained by means of the mind.
Quiescence is enlightenment, because all marks have been extinguished. Non-contemplation is enlightenment, because all conditions have been left behind.
Non-practice is bodhi, because it is free from recollection. Severance is bodhi, because it abandons all views.
Detachment is bodhi, because it is free from all deluded thoughts. Obstruction is bodhi, because it obstructs all vows.
Non-entry is bodhi, because it is free from attachment. Accordance is bodhi, because it accords with suchness. Abiding is bodhi...
"Ti. Because it abides in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is bodhi. Because it reaches the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it is bodhi.
Non-duality is bodhi, because it is free from mental objects (*dharma*). Equality is bodhi, because it is equal to empty space.

The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is bodhi, because it is without arising, abiding, or ceasing. Knowledge is bodhi, because it fully understands the mental activities of sentient beings. Non-union is bodhi..."
"Ti. Because the sense bases do not meet, non-union is bodhi. Because it is free from the habitual tendencies of afflictions, the absence of location is bodhi.
Because it has no form or color, it is designated by conventional names; this is bodhi, for names are empty.
It is like a magical creation, because there is nothing to be grasped or abandoned. It is without distraction, because it is eternally quiescent. It is perfectly tranquil."
This is bodhi, because its nature is pure. This is bodhi, because it is free from grasping. This is bodhi, because it is free from objective conditions (*ālambana*).
This is bodhi, because all phenomena are equal. This is bodhi, because it is beyond comparison. This is bodhi, because there is nothing with which it can be likened.
This is bodhi, because all phenomena are difficult to know. World-Honored One, when Vimalakīrti spoke this Dharma, two...
A hundred devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness. The Buddha said to the youth Prabhāvyūha, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Prabhāvyūha said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, I am not capable of going to him to inquire after his illness. Why is this? As I recall..."
Once, when I was departing from the great city of Vaiśālī, Vimalakīrti was entering the city.
I immediately paid him homage and asked, "Householder, from where have you come? He replied to me, "I have come from the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa)."
I asked, "What is this so-called site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa)? He replied: "The straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment, because it is free from falsehood.
The practice of resolve is the site of enlightenment, because it can accomplish all tasks. The profound mind is the site of enlightenment, because it increases merit and virtue.
The bodhicitta is the site of enlightenment, because it is free from error. Generosity is the site of enlightenment... [text continues]
The precepts are the site of awakening because they are not for the sake of seeking reward. Patience is the site of awakening because it fulfills one's vows.
Diligence is the site of awakening because the mind is unimpeded toward all sentient beings.
Meditation is the site of awakening because the mind is harmonious and supple. Wisdom is the site of awakening because of the direct perception of all phenomena. Compassion...
This is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because it treats all sentient beings with equality. Compassion is the site of enlightenment, because it endures weariness and suffering.

Joy is the site of enlightenment, because it delights in the Dharma. Equanimity is the site of enlightenment, because it severs both hatred and attachment. Supernormal powers are the site of enlightenment.
The place of enlightenment is liberation, because it brings about the accomplishment of the six supernormal powers.

The place of enlightenment is skillful means, because it enables one to turn away from and relinquish [attachment]. The place of enlightenment is the four methods of attraction, because they gather in sentient beings.

The place of enlightenment is extensive learning, because one acts in accordance with what has been heard. The place of enlightenment is the subduing of the mind, because one correctly contemplates all phenomena. Thirty.

The seven factors of awakening are the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because they abandon conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). The Four Noble Truths are the site of enlightenment, because they do not deceive the world.
Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is the site of enlightenment, because from ignorance (*avidyā*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), all are inexhaustible.

All afflictions (*kleśa*) are the site of enlightenment, because one knows them as they truly are. Sentient beings (*sattva*) are the site of enlightenment, because one knows them to be without self (*anātman*).
All dharmas are the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because one knows that all dharmas are empty. Subduing Māra is the site of enlightenment, because it is unshakable.
The three realms are the site of enlightenment, because there is nowhere to go. The lion’s roar is the site of enlightenment, because there is no fear.
The powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are the site of enlightenment, because they are free from all faults. The three knowledges (*vidyā*)...

This is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because there is no further obstruction. To know all dharmas in a single thought-moment is the site of enlightenment, because it accomplishes all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

Thus, son of good family, when a bodhisattva accords with the *pāramitās* to teach and transform sentient beings, whatever they do—whether lifting or lowering their feet—one should know that it all proceeds from the site of enlightenment.
They abide in the Buddha-dharma. When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred devas and humans all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīdhara: "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness. Dhāraṇīdhara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness. Why is this?
I recall that once, while I was staying in a quiet chamber, Māra Pāpīyān approached me with twelve thousand celestial maidens, appearing like Śakra..."
Śakra (the image) arrived at my dwelling accompanied by his retinue, with drums, music, stringed instruments, and song.
He bowed his head at my feet, joined his palms in reverence, and stood to one side. I thought he was Śakra and said to him: "Welcome, Kauśika!
Although you possess the fruits of merit, you should not indulge in self-indulgence; you should contemplate the impermanence of the five desires."
Seeking the roots of goodness, he practiced the steadfast Dharma with his body, life, and wealth, and spoke to me, saying:
"Noble sir, accept these twelve thousand celestial maidens to serve as your attendants.
I replied, "Kauśika, do not offer such unrighteous things to me, a śramaṇa son of the Śākyas; this is not appropriate for me. Before these words were even finished—
When I had finished speaking, Vimalakīrti came to me and said, "This is not Śakra; it is Māra who has come to harass and trouble you.
He then addressed Māra, saying, "These maidens may be given to me; as I am a śramaṇa, how could I not accept them?
Māra was immediately struck with fear and thought, "Vimalakīrti will surely trouble me. Desiring to vanish from sight and depart, he—
He was unable to hide; even by exhausting all his supernatural powers, he could not depart. Then, a voice from the air was heard, saying:
"Pāpīyān, give these women to him, and only then may you go. Out of fear, Māra reluctantly gave them to him.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to the women, "Māra has given you to me; now you must all..."

They resolved their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. [The Bodhisattva] then preached the Dharma to them according to what was appropriate—observing whether their faculties were sharp or dull—causing them to give rise to the aspiration for the Way.
He further said: "Now that you have all resolved your minds on the Way, there is the joy of the Dharma (*dharma-rati*) with which you may find delight;
you should no longer take pleasure in the joys of the five desires. The goddess then asked: "What is meant by the joy of the Dharma?"
He replied: "I delight in constant faith in the Buddha; I delight in wishing to hear the Dharma; I delight in making offerings to the Saṅgha;

I delight in renouncing the five desires; I delight in viewing the five aggregates as enemies and thieves; I delight in viewing the four elements as venomous snakes; I delight in viewing the internal sense bases as an empty village;
I delight in following and protecting the resolve for enlightenment; I delight in benefiting sentient beings; and I delight in reverently supporting my teachers."
He practices extensively in giving; he delights in firmly upholding the precepts; he delights in patience and gentleness; he delights in diligently accumulating roots of goodness;
he delights in meditative concentration without distraction; he delights in stainless, luminous wisdom; he delights in expanding the bodhicitta; he delights in subduing all māras;
he delights in severing all afflictions; he delights in purifying buddha-fields; and he cultivates [these] for the sake of accomplishing the primary and secondary marks.

All these virtues consist in delighting in the adornment of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), delighting in hearing the profound Dharma without fear, delighting in the three gates of liberation while not delighting in improper times,
delighting in associating with fellow students, and delighting in having a mind free from resentment or obstruction even toward those who are not fellow students.

Delighting in protecting against evil associates, delighting in associating with virtuous friends, delighting in a joyful and pure mind, and delighting in cultivating the immeasurable factors of the path—this is the Dharma-delight of a bodhisattva.
Thereupon, Pāpīyān said to the women, "I wish to return to the celestial palace together with you. The women replied, "Give us to him..."
“Householder, we have a joy in the Dharma that we greatly delight in; we no longer delight in the pleasures of the five desires.
Māra said, “Householder, you may release these women. One who gives away all they possess is a bodhisattva.
Vimalakīrti replied, “I have already given them away. You may take them with you and let all sentient beings enjoy them.”
Having attained the fulfillment of their aspirations for the Dharma, the women then asked Vimalakīrti, "How should we abide in the palace of Māra?
Vimalakīrti replied, "Sisters, there is a Dharma gate called the 'Inexhaustible Lamp' (*akṣayapradīpa*);
you should study it. As for the Inexhaustible Lamp, it is like a single lamp lighting hundreds of thousands of lamps; thus, all that was dark becomes bright."

Their illumination never comes to an end. Sisters, it is thus: when a single bodhisattva guides and instructs hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, his own resolve for that path does not diminish or cease.
Furthermore, according to the Dharma he preaches, he himself increases all wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*). This is called "inexhaustibility."

It is a lamp. Although you dwell in the palace of Māra, by means of this inexhaustible lamp, you cause countless sons and daughters of the gods to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is how you repay the Buddha’s kindness.
He also brings great benefit to all sentient beings. At that time, the goddess bowed her head at the feet of Vimalakīrti and, returning with Māra to her palace, suddenly vanished.
"World-Honored One, Vimalakīrti possesses such sovereign spiritual power, wisdom, and eloquence; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness."
The Buddha said to the elder’s son, Śrītejas, “Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Śrītejas replied to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, I am not capable of going to him to inquire after his illness. Why is this?
I recall that in the past, while at my father’s house, I established a great assembly for almsgiving to provide offerings to all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.”
At the gate, there were various non-Buddhists, the poor and lowly, and solitary beggars.
When the seven days had elapsed, Vimalakīrti entered the assembly and said to me, "Son of a noble family, a great sacrificial assembly such as you have arranged is not appropriate.
It should be an assembly for the gift of Dharma; what use is there for an assembly consisting of material gifts?"

I said to the householder, "What is called the assembly for the gift of Dharma? The assembly for the gift of Dharma is that which, without before or after, simultaneously makes offerings to all sentient beings;
this is called the assembly for the gift of Dharma. He asked, "What does this mean?"
That is to say: one arouses the mind of loving-kindness by means of bodhicitta; one arouses the mind of great compassion by means of rescuing sentient beings;

one arouses the mind of sympathetic joy by means of upholding the true Dharma; one practices the mind of equanimity by means of gathering wisdom; and one [practices it] by means of gathering those who are stingy and greedy.
One arouses the *dānapāramitā* to transform those who violate the precepts; one arouses the *śīlapāramitā* by means of the dharma of non-self;
one arouses the *kṣāntipāramitā* by means of being detached from the marks of body and mind; one arouses the *vīryapāramitā* by means of the mark of bodhi;
one arouses the *dhyānapāramitā* by means of all-knowledge; and one arouses the *prajñāpāramitā*.
He practices the pāramitās. He gives rise to emptiness while transforming sentient beings; he gives rise to signlessness without abandoning conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*);
he manifests birth while giving rise to wishlessness. He gives rise to the power of skillful means to protect and uphold the true Dharma and to deliver sentient beings.
He gives rise to the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to respectfully serve all. He gives rise to the method for removing pride regarding the body.
Regarding life and wealth, one gives rise to the three steadfast dharmas. Within the six recollections, one gives rise to the dharma of mindfulness and reflection.

Within the six points of respectful harmony, one gives rise to a mind of straightforwardness and practices the wholesome dharmas correctly. One gives rise to pure livelihood through a heart of purity and joy.

One gives rise to proximity with the noble and holy by not harboring hatred for others. One gives rise to a disciplined mind through the dharma of renunciation, thereby giving rise to the profound resolve.

One gives rise to extensive learning by practicing according to what has been taught; one gives rise to dwelling in secluded places through the dharma of non-contention; one gives rise to meditative seclusion by advancing toward the wisdom of the Buddha;
one gives rise to the stages of cultivation by untying the bonds of sentient beings; and one gives rise to the possession of the primary and secondary marks [of a Buddha].

Furthermore, they purify Buddha-fields, giving rise to the karma of merit; they know the mental inclinations of all sentient beings and preach the Dharma according to their needs, giving rise to the karma of wisdom;
they know all phenomena without grasping or rejecting, entering the gate of the single characteristic, giving rise to the karma of insight;
and they sever all afflictions, all obstacles, and all unwholesome dharmas, giving rise to...
All wholesome karma leads to the attainment of all-encompassing wisdom; all wholesome dharmas give rise to all factors that assist the path to Buddhahood.
In this way, son of good family, this is the assembly for the gift of Dharma.
If a bodhisattva abides in this assembly for the gift of Dharma, they become a great donor and a field of merit for the entire world.
World-Honored One, when Vimalakīrti preached this Dharma, two hundred people from among the assembly of brahmins all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, my mind attained purity, and I marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
