I bowed my head to pay homage at Vimalakīrti’s feet and immediately untied my necklace, worth hundreds of thousands [of gold pieces].
When he had finished speaking, Vimalakīrti refused to accept it. I said to the householder, "I pray that you will certainly accept it; give it as you please.

Vimalakīrti then accepted the necklace, divided it into two portions, took one portion and gave it to the lowliest beggar in this assembly, and took the other portion and offered it to the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha. The entire assembly—

Everyone saw the Tathāgata Duṣpradharṣa of the land of Prabhāsa, and they also saw the pearl necklace above that Buddha transform into a four-pillared jeweled terrace, magnificently adorned on all four sides and transparent so as not to obstruct one another. At that time, Vimalakīrti...
Having manifested these supernatural transformations, he further spoke these words:

"If a donor gives with an impartial mind to even the lowliest beggar, regarding them as possessing the very same characteristics of a field of merit as the Tathāgata—without making distinctions, equalizing their compassion, and seeking no karmic reward—this is called the fulfillment of the gift of Dharma. At that time, there was a lowliest beggar in the city...
Having seen this supernatural power and heard what was said, they all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Therefore, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness. Thus, each of these bodhisattvas spoke to the Buddha regarding their own past causes and conditions, recounting the words of Vimalakīrti, and all said: "I am not fit to go there."
Inquiring after Illness.
The Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Five:
Chapter on Inquiring after Illness.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, that superior man is difficult to engage in dialogue with;

he has profoundly penetrated the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), is skilled in expounding the essential points of the Dharma, possesses unimpeded eloquence, and his wisdom is without obstruction regarding all bodhisattva dharmas."
He fully understands all things. There is no secret treasury of the Buddhas that he has not entered. He has subdued the various māras (the four māras).

He sports with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), and both his wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*) have already reached the further shore. Nevertheless, he shall now follow the holy command of the Buddha and go to inquire after his illness.
Thereupon, among the assembly, the bodhisattvas, the great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings were all...
They thought to themselves: "Now these two great beings, Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti, are conversing together; they must surely be expounding the sublime Dharma.
At that moment, eight thousand bodhisattvas, five hundred śrāvakas, and hundreds of thousands of devas and humans all desired to follow them.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, together with the assembly of bodhisattvas, great disciples, and all...
Surrounded by devas and humans who paid him respectful homage, he entered the great city of Vaiśālī.
At that time, the householder Vimalakīrti thought to himself, "Now Mañjuśrī is coming with a great assembly.
He immediately used his supernormal powers to empty the interior of his room, removing all furnishings and attendants, leaving only a single couch for his illness.
Vimalakīrti was reclining. Mañjuśrī, having entered his house, saw that the chamber was empty and devoid of all possessions;
he alone was sleeping upon a single bed. Then Vimalakīrti said, "Welcome, Mañjuśrī! You have come with the aspect of not-coming;
you have seen with the aspect of not-seeing. Mañjuśrī replied, "It is so, householder. If one has already come..."
They do not come again; once gone, they do not go again (clarifying the absence of the characteristics of coming and going). Why is this? That which comes has nowhere from which it comes;
that which goes has nowhere to which it goes. What can be seen cannot be seen again. Let us set this matter aside for now.
"Householder, can this illness be endured? Is there improvement from your treatment, and has it not worsened?
The World-Honored One sends his inquiries most earnestly and boundlessly. Householder, what is the cause of this illness? How long has it been since its onset?"
"How is it extinguished? Vimalakīrti replied, "My illness arises from ignorance and craving.
Because all sentient beings are ill, I am ill. If all sentient beings were free from illness, then my illness would be extinguished.
Why is this? It is for the sake of sentient beings that a bodhisattva enters the cycle of birth and death; as long as there is birth..."
Death is accompanied by illness. If sentient beings were able to be free from illness, then Bodhisattvas would likewise no longer have illness.
It is like an elder who has but one son: if the son falls ill, the parents also fall ill;
if the son’s illness is cured, the parents are also cured. So it is with the Bodhisattva; toward all sentient beings, they love them as their own children. All...
When they fall ill, the Bodhisattva falls ill; when the illnesses of sentient beings are cured, the Bodhisattva is also cured.
Furthermore, it was asked: "From what cause does this illness arise? The Bodhisattva’s illness arises from great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Mañjuśrī said: "Householder, why is this room empty and devoid of attendants? Vimalakīrti replied: "The Buddha-fields of all Buddhas are likewise [empty]."
Furthermore, all are empty. He asked again, "By what are they empty? He replied, "They are empty by means of the emptiness of emptiness.
He asked again, "For what purpose is emptiness made empty? He replied, "It is empty because it is the emptiness of non-discrimination. He asked again, "Can emptiness be discriminated?"
He replied, "Discrimination is also empty. He asked again, "Where should emptiness be sought?
He replied, "It should be sought within the sixty-two views. He asked again, "Where should the sixty-two views be sought?
He replied, "They should be sought within the liberation of all Buddhas. He asked again, "Where should the liberation of all Buddhas be sought? He replied:
He replied: "One should seek it within the mental activities of all sentient beings. Furthermore, regarding your question as to why there is no attendant:
all Māras and all those of external paths are my attendants. Why is this?
Because the Māras delight in birth and death, and the Bodhisattva does not abandon birth and death; those of external paths delight in various..."
[The Buddha] saw that the Bodhisattva was unmoved by any views. Mañjuśrī asked, "Householder, what are the characteristics of your illness?
Vimalakīrti replied, "My illness is formless and invisible. He asked again, "Is this illness conjoined with the body, or is it conjoined with the mind?
He answered, "It is not conjoined with the body, because the characteristics of the body are detached from it; nor is it..."

The mind is unified, for the mind is like an illusion. He asked again: "Regarding the great element of earth, the great element of water, the great element of fire, and the great element of wind—among these four great elements, which one is the sickness?
He replied: "This sickness is not the great element of earth, yet it is not separate from the great element of earth."
The great elements of water, fire, and wind are likewise thus. The illnesses of sentient beings arise from these four great elements;
because they have illness, I too have illness. At that time, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti, "How should a bodhisattva console a sick bodhisattva?
Vimalakīrti replied, "One should speak of the impermanence of the body."
He does not speak of revulsion toward the body, but speaks of the body as having suffering; he does not speak of delighting in nirvāṇa, but speaks of the body as being without self;
yet he speaks of teaching and guiding sentient beings, and speaks of the body as empty and quiescent, rather than speaking of ultimate cessation.

One should speak of repenting for past transgressions, yet not speak of entering the past. Out of compassion for others' ailments as one’s own, one should recognize the suffering of countless kalpas in previous lives;
one should resolve to benefit all sentient beings, recollect the merit one has cultivated, and mindfully attend to a pure livelihood.
One must not give rise to sorrow or affliction, but should always arouse diligence and act as a physician.
"O King, just as one treats various illnesses, a bodhisattva should likewise console and encourage a sick bodhisattva, causing them to rejoice.
Mañjuśrī asked, "Householder, how does a sick bodhisattva discipline their mind?
Vimalakīrti replied, "A sick bodhisattva should form this thought: 'This illness of mine now is entirely...'"
It arises from the delusions, inversions, and various afflictions of past lives; there is no real dharma here. Who is it that suffers from illness? Why is this so?
Because it is a combination of the four great elements, it is conventionally designated as a "body. The four great elements have no master, and the body likewise has no self.
Furthermore, the arising of this illness is entirely due to attachment to a self; therefore, one should not give rise to [attachment] toward the self.
[End of section]. Having understood the root of the disease, one should immediately eliminate the notion of a self (*ātman*) and the notion of sentient beings (*sattva*).

One should instead give rise to the notion of phenomena (*dharma*). One should form this thought: "This body is merely composed of a collection of various phenomena; its arising is solely the arising of phenomena, and its cessation is solely the cessation of phenomena.
Furthermore, these phenomena are each unaware of one another; when they arise, they do not say, 'I am arising,' and when they cease, they do not..."
Regarding the statement "I shall extinguish [it]," a sick bodhisattva, in order to extinguish the notion of dharmas (*dharmasaṃjñā*), should form this thought:
"This notion of dharmas is itself a perversion (*viparyāsa*). Perversion is precisely a great affliction; I should abandon it. How does one abandon it?
By abandoning "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to self" (*ātmīya*). How does one abandon "self" and "what belongs to self"? It means abandoning these two dharmas. How...
What is it to be free from these two dharmas? It means not dwelling on internal or external dharmas, but practicing equanimity.
What is equanimity? It is the equality of the self and nirvāṇa. Why is this so?
Because both the self and nirvāṇa are empty. By what are they empty? They are empty merely by way of designation. Thus, these two dharmas lack any fixed reality.
By nature, he attains this equanimity. He has no other illness; there is only the illness of emptiness, and even that illness of emptiness is empty.
This sick bodhisattva experiences all sensations through non-appropriation. While not yet fully possessing the Buddha-dharmas, he does not extinguish sensation to realize enlightenment.
Even if his body suffers pain, he brings to mind the beings of the evil realms and gives rise to great compassion.
"Mind, since I have already tamed myself, I shall likewise tame all sentient beings. I shall eliminate their illness without eliminating the phenomena themselves;
I shall instruct them in order to sever the root of their illness. What is called the root of illness? It is the presence of objective grasping (*ālambana*).
From the presence of objective grasping comes the root of illness. What is it that is grasped? It is the three realms. Thus he spoke.
How does one sever clinging? By means of non-apprehension. If there is no apprehension, then there is no clinging. What is meant by non-apprehension?
It means being free from the two views. What are the two views? They are the view of the internal and the view of the external; this is non-apprehension.
Mañjuśrī, this is how a sick bodhisattva disciplines his mind in order to sever [clinging].
The suffering of old age, sickness, and death—this is the bodhi of a bodhisattva. If it were not so, the cultivation and practice one has undertaken would be of no wise benefit.

Just as one is called brave only when one has conquered a superior enemy, so too is one called a bodhisattva when they simultaneously eliminate old age, sickness, and death. That sick bodhisattva should further reflect: "As for me..."
This illness is neither real nor existent; the illnesses of sentient beings are likewise neither real nor existent.
When contemplating in this way, if one gives rise to a great compassion based on attachment or views toward sentient beings, one should immediately abandon it. Why is this?
The Bodhisattva eliminates adventitious afflictions and gives rise to great compassion. Those whose compassion arises from attachment and views develop weariness toward birth and death;
if one can remain free from these, there will be no weariness, and wherever one is born, [one remains steadfast].
They are not shrouded by craving or views. Their births are without bondage, and they are able to preach the Dharma for sentient beings to liberate them from their bonds.
As the Buddha has said: "If one is oneself bound, it is impossible that one could liberate the bonds of others."
If one is oneself unbound, one can release the bonds of others; this is indeed possible. Therefore, a bodhisattva should not give rise to bondage.
What is called bondage? What is called liberation? Attachment to the flavor of dhyāna is the bondage of a bodhisattva.
To be born through skillful means is the liberation of a bodhisattva. Furthermore, wisdom without skillful means is bondage; wisdom with skillful means is liberation. There is no... [text ends]
There is bondage by means of wisdom and skillful means; there is liberation by means of wisdom and skillful means. What is meant by being bound by wisdom lacking skillful means?

It refers to a bodhisattva who, with a mind of attachment and false views, adorns buddha-fields and brings sentient beings to maturity, yet seeks to discipline himself within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
This is called being bound by wisdom lacking skillful means. What is meant by having skillful means...

This is liberation through wisdom and skillful means. That is to say, one adorns the Buddha-lands and brings sentient beings to maturity not with a mind of craving or views, but within the sphere of the empty, signless, and wishless, self-subduing without weariness;
this is called liberation through wisdom and skillful means. What is bondage through lack of wisdom and skillful means? It refers to a bodhisattva dwelling in desire and hatred...
To plant the roots of all virtues while still possessing afflictions such as anger and wrong views—this is called "bondage through lack of wisdom and skillful means.

What is meant by "liberation through wisdom and skillful means"? It refers to planting the roots of all virtues while remaining free from afflictions such as greed, anger, and wrong views, and dedicating them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Ānanda, this is called liberation through wisdom and skillful means. Mañjuśrī, that sick bodhisattva should contemplate all phenomena in this way.
Furthermore, he contemplates the body as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; this is called wisdom.
Although his body is ill, he remains constantly within the cycle of birth and death to benefit all beings, never wearying or becoming exhausted."
This is called skillful means (*upāya*). Furthermore, one contemplates the body: the body is not separate from illness, and illness is not separate from the body.
This illness and this body are neither new nor old; this is called wisdom (*prajñā*). Even if the body has an ailment, it does not undergo ultimate extinction;
this is called skillful means. Mañjuśrī, a sick bodhisattva should thus discipline his mind.
He does not abide within them, nor does he abide in an undisciplined mind. Why is this?
To abide in an undisciplined mind is the way of fools; to abide in a disciplined mind is the way of the śrāvakas.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should not abide in either a disciplined or an undisciplined mind. Being free from these two dharmas—this is [the path].
The bodhisattva practice is to remain within birth and death without being defiled by conduct; it is to abide in nirvāṇa without entering final extinction. This is the bodhisattva practice.
It is not the practice of ordinary worldlings, nor is it the practice of noble sages. This is the bodhisattva practice. It is neither a defiled practice nor a pure practice.
This is the bodhisattva practice. Although it transcends the practices of Māra, it manifests the subduing of all [demons].
This is the bodhisattva practice: seeking all-knowledge, one does not seek it at an improper time; this is the bodhisattva practice.
Although observing that all phenomena are unarisen, one does not enter the fixed position of certainty; this is the bodhisattva practice.

Although observing the twelve links of dependent origination, one enters into [the understanding of] various false views; this is the bodhisattva practice. Although gathering in all sentient beings...
To be without attachment is the practice of a bodhisattva. Although they delight in seclusion, they do not rely on the exhaustion of body and mind; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.

Although they move within the three realms, they do not destroy the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); this is the practice of a bodhisattva. Although they move within emptiness, they plant the roots of all virtues;
this is the practice of a bodhisattva. Although they move within signlessness, they deliver sentient beings... [to liberation]. This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
To be born is the bodhisattva’s practice. To manifest the reception of a body while practicing non-action is the bodhisattva’s practice.
To initiate all wholesome deeds while practicing non-arising is the bodhisattva’s practice.
To thoroughly know the minds and mental factors of sentient beings while practicing the six pāramitās is the bodhisattva’s practice. To practice the six supernormal powers...

Yet they do not exhaust their outflows; this is the bodhisattva practice. Although they practice the four immeasurable minds, they do not crave attachment to birth in the Brahma world; this is the bodhisattva practice.
Although they practice dhyāna, liberation, and samādhi, they are not reborn according to those meditative states; this is the bodhisattva practice.
Although they practice the four foundations of mindfulness, they do not ultimately and permanently abandon the body; this is the bodhisattva practice.

To practice the mindfulness of feelings, mind, and phenomena (i.e., the four foundations of mindfulness) is the bodhisattva’s practice. Although practicing the four right efforts, not abandoning physical and mental diligence is the bodhisattva’s practice.
Although practicing the four bases of power, attaining sovereign supernormal powers is the bodhisattva’s practice.
Although practicing the five faculties, discerning the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings is the bodhisattva’s practice.
To practice the five powers while joyfully seeking the ten powers of a Buddha is the bodhisattva practice.
To practice the seven factors of awakening while discerning the wisdom of a Buddha is the bodhisattva practice.
To practice the eightfold noble path while joyfully practicing the immeasurable path of a Buddha is the bodhisattva practice. To practice the aids to the path of tranquility and insight...
To practice the Dharma without ultimately falling into cessation is the bodhisattva’s practice.
To practice all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, yet to adorn one's body with the marks and signs of excellence, is the bodhisattva’s practice.
To manifest the deportment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, yet not abandon the Buddha-dharma, is the bodhisattva’s practice. Although following...
To manifest one's body according to what is appropriate, while all phenomena are ultimately characterized by purity—this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although they contemplate that the buddha-fields are eternally quiescent like space, they nevertheless manifest various kinds of pure buddha-fields.

This is the practice of a bodhisattva: although they attain the path of the Buddha, turn the wheel of Dharma, and enter nirvana, they do not abandon the path of the bodhisattva. This is the practice of a bodhisattva.
When these words were spoken, among the great assembly led by Mañjuśrī, eight thousand devaputras all resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Third, the Bodhicitta.
The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Volume Six,
Chapter on the Inconceivable.
At that time, Śāriputra, seeing that there were no seats within this room, thought to himself:
"Where shall these bodhisattvas and the great assembly of disciples sit? The elder Vimalakīrti, knowing his thoughts, [spoke].
He said to Śāriputra, "How is it, Venerable One? Have you come for the sake of the Dharma, or do you seek a seat?
Śāriputra replied, "I have come for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of a seat.
Vimalakīrti said, "Indeed, Śāriputra, one who seeks the Dharma does not even covet their own body or life, let alone a seat. Truly, one who seeks the Dharma..."
There is seeking after form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; there is no seeking after the elements (dhātus) or the sense bases (āyatanas);

there is no seeking after desire, form, or formlessness (that is, no seeking within the three realms). Śāriputra, one who seeks the Dharma does not seek by clinging to the Buddha, does not seek by clinging to the Dharma, and does not seek by clinging to the Saṅgha.
One who seeks the Dharma has no seeking for the vision of suffering, and no seeking for the abandonment of its origin.
There is no seeking of the path of cultivation for the realization of the exhaustion of what is unconditioned. Why is this? Because phenomena are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
If one says, "I shall see suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path," this is conceptual proliferation; it is not the seeking of the Dharma.
Śāriputra, the Dharma is named "quiescence. If one practices with arising and ceasing, one is seeking arising and ceasing, not seeking the Dharma.
The Dharma is named "stainless. If one is stained by dharmas, even up to nirvāṇa, this is attachment.
This is not the seeking of the Dharma. The Dharma has no place for practice; if one practices within the Dharma, that is a place of practice, not the seeking of the Dharma.
The Dharma has no grasping or rejecting; if one grasps or rejects the Dharma, that is grasping and rejecting, not the seeking of the Dharma.
The Dharma has no location. If one clings to a location, that is clinging to a place; it is not the seeking of the Dharma. The Dharma is named "signlessness.
If one follows signs with consciousness, that is seeking signs; it is not the seeking of the Dharma. The Dharma cannot be dwelled upon.
If one dwells in phenomena (*dharma*), one is dwelling in phenomena rather than seeking the Dharma. The Dharma cannot be seen, heard, sensed, or known;
if one acts through seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, one is engaging in seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing rather than seeking the Dharma.
The Dharma is named the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); if one acts within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), one is seeking the conditioned rather than seeking the Dharma. Therefore, abandon it.
“Ānanda, if one seeks the Dharma, one should seek nothing at all regarding any phenomena.
When these words were spoken, five hundred devaputras attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti asked Mañjuśrī, “O Benevolent One, you have traveled through immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeyas of kalpas.”
“Householder, in which buddha-field is there a lion throne endowed with such excellent, sublime, and perfected qualities?
Mañjuśrī replied, “Householder, to the east, passing through lands as numerous as the sands of thirty-six Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sumeru-lakṣaṇa.
Its Buddha is named Sumeru-pradīpa-rāja, who currently resides there. That Buddha’s body...”
It was eighty-four thousand yojanas in length. Its lion throne was eighty-four thousand yojanas high, the most exquisitely adorned of all.

Then, the elder Vimalakīrti manifested his supernormal powers, and immediately that Buddha dispatched thirty-two thousand lion thrones—lofty, broad, magnificent, and pure—which entered into Vimalakīrti’s abode.
The room was such that the various bodhisattvas, great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and others had never seen before;

it was vast and expansive, fully encompassing all. Within it were thirty-two thousand lion thrones, yet there was no obstruction within the city of Vaiśālī, nor any crowding throughout Jambudvīpa and the four continents. It was entirely...
They appeared as they had before. At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Mañjuśrī, "Please take a seat upon this lion throne together with these eminent bodhisattvas;
you should manifest your own body to correspond to the form of this seat.
Thereupon, the bodhisattvas who had attained supernatural powers transformed their bodies to be forty-two thousand yojanas in height and sat upon the lion thrones.
The bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds and the great disciples were all unable to ascend it.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra, "Please take a seat upon the lion throne.
Śāriputra replied, "Householder, this seat is so high and broad that I am unable to ascend it. Vimalakīrti said, "Indeed, Śāriputra, for the sake of Sumerudīpa-rāja..."

"Only after the Tathāgata has paid homage may one take a seat. Thereupon, the bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds and the great disciples immediately paid homage to the Tathāgata Sumerudīparāja; they were then able to sit upon the lion thrones.
Śāriputra said to the layman, "It is unprecedented! How is it that such a small room can accommodate these [thrones] so high..."
The seat was vast; it did not obstruct anything within the city of Vaiśālī.
Furthermore, it did not crowd the villages, cities, and towns of Jambudvīpa, nor the palaces of the devas, nāga kings, ghosts, and spirits throughout the four continents.
Vimalakīrti said, "O Śāriputra, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess a liberation called 'Non-..."

This is inconceivable. If a bodhisattva dwells in this liberation, they can place Mount Sumeru, with its height and breadth, inside a mustard seed without it increasing or decreasing; the King of Mountains, Sumeru, remains as it was in its original form.
Yet, the Four Heavenly Kings and the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven neither perceive nor know where they have entered; only those who are ready for deliverance do so.
To see Mount Sumeru enter into a mustard seed—this is called the inconceivable Dharma-gate of liberation.

Furthermore, one may cause the waters of the four great oceans to enter a single pore without disturbing the fish, turtles, crocodiles, alligators, or other aquatic creatures, while that great ocean remains as it was by its original nature. The various dragons, spirits, and asuras therein likewise remain undisturbed.
He is unaware of where he has entered; nor does he cause any disturbance to these sentient beings.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva who dwells in this inconceivable liberation can take up the trichiliocosm and hold it.
It is like a potter’s wheel: held in the right palm, it is thrown beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

yet the sentient beings therein are neither aware nor conscious of where they have gone. Furthermore, it is returned to its original place without causing anyone to have any perception of coming or going, and this world remains exactly as it was before. Moreover, Śāriputra, [it is thus].
If there are sentient beings who delight in dwelling long in the world and can be liberated,
the Bodhisattva immediately expands seven days into one kalpa, causing those sentient beings to perceive it as a single kalpa.
If there are sentient beings who do not delight in dwelling long and can be liberated, the Bodhisattva immediately contracts one kalpa into seven days, causing them...

Sentient beings call this "seven days. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva who dwells in the inconceivable liberation can gather the adornments of all buddha-fields into a single land and show them to sentient beings.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva places all sentient beings of all buddha-fields upon his right palm and flies to the ten directions, displaying them everywhere without moving them from their original locations.

Moreover, Śāriputra, regarding the articles of offering used by sentient beings in the ten directions to honor the Buddhas, a bodhisattva causes them all to be seen within a single pore. Furthermore, the ten directions...
All the suns, moons, and stars existing within that land, he causes them all to be seen within a single pore.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, all the winds existing throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the bodhisattva is able to inhale and draw into his mouth.
Yet their bodies were not harmed, nor were the trees outside them broken or shattered.

Furthermore, when the worlds of the ten directions are consumed by fire at the end of a kalpa, they place all those fires within their bellies; the fires continue as before without causing them any injury.
Moreover, from below, passing through Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they take up a single buddha-field.
They lift it upward, passing through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as easily as one might lift a jujube leaf with the point of a needle,
without causing it any disturbance. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva dwelling in this inconceivable liberation can,
by means of supernormal powers, manifest the body of a Buddha, or manifest the body of a pratyekabuddha, or manifest the body of a śrāvaka...
Regarding the body of hearing: he may manifest the body of Śakra, or the body of Brahmā, or the body of a world-protector, or the body of a wheel-turning sage king (*cakravartin*).

Furthermore, all sounds throughout the worlds of the ten directions—whether superior, middling, or inferior—he is able to transform them all so that they become the voice of the Buddha, proclaiming impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
...sounds, as well as the various teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions, all of which he causes others to hear universally within that [samādhi].
Śāriputra, I have now briefly explained the power of the inconceivable liberation of a bodhisattva.
Were it to be explained in detail, it would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon. At that time, Mahākāśyapa heard this discourse on the bodhisattva...
"This Dharma-door of the inconceivable liberation is truly marvelous!
O Śāriputra, it is like a person who displays various forms and images before those who are blind; these are not seen by them. So it is with all śrāvakas."
It is because they have heard this inconceivable Dharma-door of liberation and yet are unable to comprehend it that they remain as they are.
When the wise hear this, who among them would not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
"Why have we eternally severed our roots? Regarding this Mahāyāna, we are like withered seeds.
All Śrāvakas, upon hearing this inconceivable Dharma-door of liberation, should wail and weep until their voices shake the trichiliocosm;
all Bodhisattvas should rejoice greatly and receive this Dharma upon the crowns of their heads."
"If there are bodhisattvas who have faith and understanding in this inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation, all the hosts of Māras will be powerless against them.
When Mahākāśyapa spoke these words, thirty-two thousand devaputras [attained realization].
All of them resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Mahākāśyapa:

"O Noble One, among those who act as Māras in immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya worlds throughout the ten directions, most are bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation who, by means of skillful power, provide instruction."

To transform sentient beings, he manifests as a Māra king. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, there may be someone who begs from immeasurable Bodhisattvas of the ten directions for their hands, feet, ears, or noses;
their heads, eyes, marrow, or brains; their blood, flesh, skin, or bones; their villages, cities, or towns;
their wives, children, servants, or slaves; or their elephants, horses, carriages, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, or coral.

Pearls, amber, true pearls, conch shells, clothing, food, and drink—those who beg for such things are mostly bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation who, by the power of skillful means, go to test them in order to make their resolve firm. Why is this?
Because bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation possess majestic authority.
Therefore, they exercise coercion and demonstrate such difficult tasks to all sentient beings.
Ordinary people of inferior capacity lack the power and influence to thus coerce a bodhisattva; it is like the trampling of a dragon-elephant, which a donkey cannot endure.
This is called the wisdom and skillful means of a bodhisattva dwelling in inconceivable liberation.
The Gate of [the Tathāgata].
The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Seven:
Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings.
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti, "How does a bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings?
Vimalakīrti replied, "It is like a magician looking at a person created by his own magic; a bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings in this way.
It is like a wise man looking at the moon in water, or like seeing the reflection of one's own face in a mirror."
Like a mirage in the heat, like an echo, like clouds in the sky, like a mass of foam, like bubbles on the water,
like the solidity of a plantain tree, like lightning that lasts long, like a fifth great element, like a sixth aggregate,
like a seventh sense-organ, like a thirteenth base, and like a nineteenth realm— thus does the Bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings.
This is like form in the formless realm; like the sprout of parched grain; like the view of a self in the body of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*);

like the entry into a womb by a non-returner (*anāgāmin*); like the three poisons in an arhat; like the greed, anger, and violation of precepts in a bodhisattva who has attained patient acceptance (*kṣānti*);
like the habitual tendencies of afflictions in a Buddha; like a blind person seeing forms; and like the entering and emerging from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
It is like the tracks of a bird in the sky; like the son of a barren woman; like the afflictions of a magically conjured person;
like seeing something in a dream upon waking; like a deceased person receiving a body; like a fire without smoke.
Thus does a bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings. Mañjuśrī asked: "If a bodhisattva contemplates in this way, how [should they act]?"
He practices loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Vimalakīrti said: "When a bodhisattva has made this contemplation, he thinks to himself:
'I shall preach such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings. This is true loving-kindness. He practices the loving-kindness of cessation (*śānti*), because there is nothing that arises.

He practices the unfeverish loving-kindness, because there are no afflictions (*kleśa*). He practices impartial loving-kindness, because it is equal throughout the three periods of time. He practiced...
He practices the compassion of non-contention, because there is nothing that arises. He practices the compassion of non-duality, because the internal and external do not meet.
He practices the unbreakable compassion, because it is ultimately exhaustive. He practices the firm compassion, because the mind is indestructible. He practices the pure compassion.
Because all phenomena are pure by nature, one practices boundless compassion. Because it is like space, one practices the compassion of an Arhat;
because it destroys the thieves of the fetters, one practices the compassion of a Bodhisattva; because it establishes sentient beings [in peace], one practices the compassion of a Tathāgata;

because one has attained the mark of suchness, one practices the compassion of a Buddha (who is called "Buddha" because he awakens himself and awakens others); because he awakens sentient beings, one practices spontaneous compassion; because it is obtained without cause, one practices natural compassion.

They practice the compassion of awakening because it is of a single, equal flavor (that is, equal and signless). They practice incomparable compassion because it severs all craving. They practice the compassion of great pity because it guides by means of the Mahāyāna.
They practice tireless compassion because they contemplate emptiness and non-self. They practice the compassion of the gift of Dharma because they have no regret or withholding.
They practice the compassion of upholding the precepts because they transform those who violate the prohibitions. They practice the compassion of patience...

One practices the compassion of diligence in order to protect both oneself and others. One practices the compassion of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in order to bear the burden of sentient beings.

One practices the compassion of wisdom (*prajñā*) because one does not relish flavors (the flavors of the five desires). One practices the compassion of skillful means (*upāya*) because there is nothing that is not manifested at the appropriate time.
One practices the compassion of non-concealment because the straightforward mind is pure. One practices the compassion of the profound mind because it is unmixed with defilements.

Because they practice, they cultivate the compassion that is free from deception; because it is not false or artificial. Because they practice, they cultivate the compassion that brings peace and happiness;
because it causes others to attain the bliss of the Buddhas. Such is the compassion of a bodhisattva. Mañjuśrī then asked again, "What is meant by 'compassion' (karuṇā)?
He replied, "Whatever merits a bodhisattva has performed, he shares them all with all sentient beings. What?
"What is meant by joy? He replied, "To bring benefit to others with a joyful heart and without regret. "What is meant by equanimity?
He replied, "To perform meritorious deeds without harboring any expectations. Mañjuśrī asked again, "In the face of the terrors of birth and death, upon what should a bodhisattva rely?
Vimalakīrti said, "Regarding the terrors of birth and death, the bodhisattva..."
"One should rely upon the power of the Tathāgata’s merits. Mañjuśrī asked again, "If a bodhisattva wishes to rely upon the power of the Tathāgata’s merits, in what should they abide?
He replied, "A bodhisattva who wishes to rely upon the power of the Tathāgata’s merits should abide in the liberation of all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī asked again, "And how does one wish to liberate sentient beings?"
"What should be eliminated? He replied, "One who wishes to deliver sentient beings must eliminate their afflictions (*kleśa*).
Again he asked, "If one wishes to eliminate afflictions, what should one practice? He replied, "One should practice right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
Again he asked, "How does one practice right mindfulness? He replied, "One should practice non-arising and non-ceasing. Again he asked, "What dharma does not arise? What dharma..."
"It is not extinguished. He replied, "The unwholesome does not arise; wholesome dharmas are not extinguished. He asked again, "What is the root of the wholesome and the unwholesome?
He replied, "The body is the root. He asked again, "What is the root of the body?
He replied, "Craving and greed are the root. He asked again, "What is the root of craving and greed? He replied, "False conceptualization is the root. He asked again.
"What is the root of false discrimination? He replied, "Inverted perception is its root. He asked again, "What is the root of inverted perception?
He replied, "Non-abiding is its root. He asked again, "What is the root of non-abiding?
He replied, "Non-abiding has no root. Mañjuśrī, from this root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established."
At that time, in the room of Vimalakīrti, there was a celestial maiden who, seeing the various devas and humans and hearing the Dharma being preached, manifested her form.
She then took celestial flowers and scattered them over the bodhisattvas and great disciples. When the flowers reached the bodhisattvas, they all fell away;
but when they reached the great disciples, they stuck to them and did not fall. Thus it was with all the disciples.
He used his supernormal power to remove the flowers, but was unable to make them go. Then the deva asked Śāriputra, "For what reason do you remove these flowers?
He replied, "These flowers are not in accordance with the Dharma; therefore, I remove them. The deva said, "Do not say that these flowers are not in accordance with the Dharma.
Why is this? These flowers have no discrimination; it is you, O Venerable One, who conceive such thoughts."
It is merely a conceptualization of discrimination. If one who has gone forth in the Buddha-dharma harbors any discrimination, it is contrary to the Dharma;
if there is no discrimination, then it is in accordance with the Dharma. Observe the various Bodhisattvas whose flowers do not adhere to them:
this is because they have already severed all conceptualizations of discrimination. It is like when a person is afraid, and non-human spirits take advantage of that vulnerability. As it is said:
This disciple, because he fears birth and death, allows form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch to gain the advantage over him.
For one who has already abandoned fear, all five desires are powerless. While his fetters and habitual tendencies are not yet exhausted, the flowers merely cling to his body.
"For one whose habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are exhausted, flowers do not adhere. Śāriputra asked, "How long has it been since this goddess has dwelt in this room?
She replied, "I have dwelt in this room for as long as you, Venerable One, have been in liberation. Śāriputra said, "Has she dwelt here for so long?
The goddess asked, "And how long has it been since you, Venerable One, attained liberation? Śāriputra remained silent.
He did not answer. The deva said, "Why do you, an elder of great wisdom, remain silent? He replied, "One who is liberated has nothing to say;
therefore, I do not know what to speak. The deva said, "Words and letters are all the marks of liberation. Why is this so?
Liberation is neither internal nor external, nor does it exist in between the two."
Syllables are neither internal nor external, nor do they abide between the two. Therefore, Śāriputra, there is no liberation apart from syllables.
Why is this? Because all dharmas possess the characteristic of liberation.
Śāriputra said, "Is it not the case that liberation consists in being free from lust, anger, and delusion?
The goddess said, "The Buddha spoke of liberation as being free from lust, anger, and delusion only for those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
For those without overweening pride, the Buddha taught that the very nature of lust, anger, and delusion is itself liberation. Śāriputra said, "Excellent!"
"Excellent, O goddess! What have you attained? By what means have you realized this, such that your eloquence is as it is? The goddess replied, "I have neither attainment nor realization;
therefore, my eloquence is as it is. Why is this so? If one were to have attainment or realization, one would be characterized by overweening pride (*adhimāna*) regarding the Buddha-dharma.
Śāriputra asked the goddess, "Regarding the three vehicles (*triyāna*), which do you follow?"
"For what purpose do you seek this? The deva replied, "I am a śrāvaka because I transform sentient beings through the Dharma of the śrāvakas;
I am a pratyekabuddha because I transform sentient beings through the Dharma of causes and conditions;
I am of the Mahāyāna because I transform sentient beings through the Dharma of great compassion. Śāriputra, it is like a person entering a campaka grove who smells only [the scent of the campaka].

Just as the *campaka* flower does not smell other fragrances, so it is here: if one enters this room, one smells only the fragrance of the Buddha’s merits, and takes no pleasure in smelling the fragrance of the merits of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Śāriputra, if there are Śakras, Brahmās, the Four Heavenly Kings, or any among the devas, nāgas, ghosts, or spirits who enter this room, they shall hear this sublime [Dharma].
When people preach the True Dharma, they all delight in the fragrance of the Buddha’s merits and emerge having resolved their minds [for enlightenment].
Śāriputra, I have dwelt in this room for twelve years, yet from the beginning I have never heard any teaching on the Dharma of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;
I have heard only the inconceivable Dharma of the Buddhas, characterized by the great kindness and great compassion of Bodhisattvas. Śāriputra...
"Ānanda, in this room there are always eight marvelous and rare phenomena ever-present. What are these eight?
This room is constantly illuminated by golden light; day and night are no different, and it does not rely on the illumination of the sun or moon for its brightness.
This is the first marvelous and rare phenomenon. Furthermore, those who enter this room..."
It is afflicted by all manner of defilements. This is the second unprecedented and rare dharma.
This room is constantly filled with Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and Bodhisattvas from other directions, who come to assemble without ceasing.
This is the third unprecedented and rare dharma. In this room, the six pāramitās are constantly preached without regression.
The Dharma—these are the four unprecedented and rare dharmas. This room constantly produces the supreme music of devas and humans;
from its strings emerge immeasurable sounds of the transformative teachings of the Dharma—this is the fifth unprecedented and rare dharma.
Within this room are four great treasuries, filled to overflowing with all manner of jewels, used to relieve the destitute and aid the needy. Those who seek...
One attains inexhaustibility. These are the six unprecedented and rare dharmas.

Within this room reside Śākyamuni Buddha, Amitābha Buddha, Akṣobhya Buddha, Ratnaguṇa, Ratnārcis, Ratnacandra, Ratnavyūha, Durjaya, Siṃhanāda, Sarvārthasiddha, and other such immeasurable Buddhas from the ten directions.
When the Superior One thinks of them, they all come immediately. They extensively expound the secret and essential Dharma-treasuries of the Buddhas, and having finished speaking, they depart.

This is the seventh unprecedented and rare dharma. Furthermore, within this room, the adorned palaces of all the devas and the pure lands of all the Buddhas appear therein. This is the eighth unprecedented [dharma].
“Rare are these dharmas. Śāriputra, in this room there constantly appear eight rare and unprecedented dharmas.
Who, having witnessed such inconceivable matters, would still take pleasure in the Dharma of the śrāvakas?
Śāriputra said, “Why do you not transform your female body? The goddess replied, “It has been twelve years since I [have been so].”
When one seeks the marks of a woman, they are utterly unfindable; how then could there be any transformation?
Suppose, for example, a magician conjures an illusory woman by means of illusion. If someone were to ask, "Why does she not transform her female body? would that person be asking correctly?
Śāriputra replied, "No. An illusion has no fixed characteristic; how could it undergo transformation?
The goddess said, "All dharmas are likewise thus: they have no fixed characteristics. Why, then, do you ask whether she does not transform her female body?"

Immediately, by her supernatural power, the goddess transformed Śāriputra so that he appeared like a goddess, while she herself manifested a body like that of Śāriputra. She then asked him, "Why do you not transform this female body?
Śāriputra, appearing in the form of the goddess, replied, "I do not know what has been transformed to become this female body."
The goddess said: "Śāriputra, if you were able to transform this female body, then all women would likewise be able to transform theirs.
Just as you, Śāriputra, are not a woman yet manifest in a female body, so it is with all women;
though they manifest in female bodies, they are not women. For this reason, the Buddha has taught that all dharmas..."
He was neither male nor female. Immediately, the goddess withdrew her supernatural power, and Śāriputra’s body returned to its former state.
The goddess asked Śāriputra, "Where now are the physical characteristics and marks of a woman?
Śāriputra replied, "The physical characteristics and marks of a woman exist nowhere, nor do they not exist. The goddess said, "All dharmas are likewise so."
Thus it is. There is neither being nor non-being. That which is neither being nor non-being is what the Buddha has taught.
Śāriputra asked the goddess, "When you pass away from here, where will you be reborn? The goddess replied, "I shall be born as one born through the Buddha’s transformation; I am born like that.
Śāriputra said, "One born through the Buddha’s transformation is neither passing away nor being born. The goddess said, "Sentient beings..."
"It is so. It is not that I have perished and been reborn. Śāriputra asked the goddess, "How long will it be before you attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The goddess replied, "When Śāriputra returns to being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), then I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Śāriputra said, "I [shall never again] become..."

"It is impossible for an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) [to attain it]. The Devaputra said, "It is likewise impossible for me to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this? Because *bodhi* has no place of abiding;
therefore, there is no one who attains it. Śāriputra said, "Now, the Buddhas have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
Śāriputra said: "Those who have attained, and those who will attain [enlightenment], are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; what do you mean by this? Devadatta said:
"It is only because of worldly conventions and numerical designations that one speaks of the three periods of time. It does not mean that Bodhi has past, future, or present.
Devadatta said: "Śāriputra, have you attained the path of Arhatship? Śāriputra replied: "I have attained it precisely because there is nothing to be attained."
The goddess said, "All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are likewise; they attain through non-attainment.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra, "This goddess has already made offerings to ninety-two billion Buddhas.
She is able to sport with the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, her vows are fully realized, and she has attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)."
Abiding in non-retrogression, by virtue of their original vows, they are able to manifest themselves at will to teach and transform sentient beings.
*The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*, Scroll Eight,
"Chapter on the Buddha-Way."
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti, "How does a bodhisattva penetrate the path of the Buddha?
Vimalakīrti replied, "If a bodhisattva practices what is not the path, this is what constitutes penetrating the path of the Buddha."
He asked again: "How does a bodhisattva practice what is not the Way? He replied:

"If a bodhisattva practices the five acts of immediate retribution (the five heinous crimes), yet remains free from affliction and anger; if he reaches the hells, yet is free from the defilements that cause them; if he reaches the realm of animals, yet is free from the faults of ignorance, pride, and the like;
if he reaches the realm of hungry ghosts, yet is fully endowed with merit; and if he practices within the realm of form..."
They do not regard the paths of the formless realm as superior. They manifest the practice of sensual desire, yet remain free from all defiled attachments.
They manifest the practice of anger, yet harbor no resentment or obstruction toward sentient beings. They manifest the practice of ignorance, yet subdue their minds with wisdom.
They manifest the practice of stinginess and greed, yet relinquish all internal and external possessions without begrudging even their own bodies or lives.
They manifest the practice of violating the precepts, yet they abide securely in pure morality; even regarding minor transgressions, they harbor great dread.
They manifest the practice of anger, yet they are always compassionate and patient. They manifest the practice of indolence, yet they diligently cultivate meritorious virtues.

They manifest the practice of a distracted mind, yet they are constantly mindful of meditative concentration. They manifest the practice of ignorance, yet they penetrate both the mundane and the supramundane.
With wisdom, he manifests deceitful behavior, yet through skillful means he accords with the meaning of all sutras;
he manifests arrogance, yet toward sentient beings he is like a bridge; he manifests all afflictions, yet his mind is ever pure;
he manifests entry into the realm of Māra, yet he follows the Buddha’s wisdom and does not follow the teachings of others; he manifests entry among the śrāvakas, yet for...
To sentient beings, he speaks of the Dharma they have not yet heard; he manifests entry into the state of a pratyekabuddha, yet accomplishes great compassion to transform sentient beings.
He manifests entry into poverty, yet possesses a jewel-hand with inexhaustible merit. He manifests entry into physical deformity.
Yet, while being adorned with all the marks of excellence, he manifests entry among the lowly and base, yet is born into the lineage of the Buddhas and possesses all merits.
He manifests entry among the weak, inferior, and ugly, yet attains the body of Nārāyaṇa, which all sentient beings delight to behold.
He manifests entry into old age and sickness, yet forever severs the root of illness and transcends it.
He manifests the fear of death, yet he constantly contemplates impermanence and truly has nothing for which to crave.

He manifests having wives, concubines, and female attendants, yet he always remains far removed from the mire of the five desires. He appears dull-witted, yet he achieves eloquence and possesses unerring dhāraṇī-retention.
He manifests entry into heterodox paths, yet he delivers all sentient beings by means of the true path.
He manifests entry into all paths while severing their causal conditions; he manifests nirvāṇa while not severing birth and death.
Mañjuśrī, when a bodhisattva can thus practice upon what is not the path, this is called penetrating the Buddha-way.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti asked Mañjuśrī, "What constitutes the lineage of the Tathāgata?"
Mañjuśrī said: “The body is a seed; ignorance and craving for existence are seeds; greed, hatred, and delusion are seeds;
the four inversions are seeds; the five hindrances are seeds; the six sense bases are seeds; the seven stations of consciousness are seeds;
the eightfold wrong path is a seed; the nine grounds for resentment are seeds; and the ten unwholesome paths of action are seeds.”
To state it briefly: the sixty-two views and all afflictions (*kleśa*) are all seeds of the Buddha. It was asked, "What does this mean?

He replied, "If one perceives the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and enters the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), they can no longer give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It is like a high plateau or dry land, where lotuses do not grow."
A lotus flower grows from low-lying, damp mud. In the same way, those who perceive unconditioned dharmas and enter the stage of correctness can never again give rise to the Buddha-dharma;
it is only within the mire of afflictions that sentient beings can produce the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, just as planting a seed in empty space can never result in growth, whereas in soil enriched with manure...
It can cause them to flourish. In this same way, those who have entered the unconditioned state of correctness do not give rise to the Buddha-dharma;
yet even if they harbor a view of self as large as Mount Sumeru, they are still able to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and produce the Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, one should know that all afflictions are the seeds of the Tathāgata. For example:

"Just as one cannot obtain a priceless jewel without descending into the great ocean, so too, one cannot obtain the jewel of omniscience without entering the great ocean of afflictions. At that time, Mahākāśyapa exclaimed, "Excellent, excellent!
Mañjuśrī, you have spoken these words most skillfully; it is truly as you have said. Of the dust-like afflictions—"
...of the Tathāgata’s lineage. We are no longer capable of resolving to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Even those who have committed the five sins of immediate retribution are still able to conceive the aspiration to be born within the Buddha-dharma;
yet we are forever incapable of conceiving it. It is like a man whose sense organs are destroyed; as for him—
The five desires can no longer bring benefit. Likewise, for a śrāvaka who has severed all fetters, there is nothing further to be gained within the Buddha-dharma;

they will never again aspire to it. Therefore, Mañjuśrī, ordinary worldlings may still turn back toward the Buddha-dharma, whereas śrāvakas do not. Why is this? Because when ordinary worldlings hear the Buddha-dharma...
One is able to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment and ensure that the Three Jewels are never severed.

Even if a śrāvaka were to hear of the Buddha-dharma, the powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth for the rest of their life, they would never be able to conceive the intention for unsurpassed enlightenment.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana (Universal Manifestation of Physical Form), who asked Vimalakīrti: "Householder, [what do you say of] parents, wife, and children?"
"Where are all these relatives and kinsmen? Where are the officials, the commoners, and acquaintances?
And where are all the slaves, servants, elephants, horses, and carriages? Thereupon, Vimalakīrti replied in verse:
The Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of Bodhisattvas; Expedient Means is their father. All Teachers of the Multitude are born from these.
Dharma-joy is their wife; Compassion and Benevolence are their daughters;
a virtuous and sincere mind is their son; Ultimate Emptiness and Quiescence are their home; and the various afflictions are their disciples.
Turning according to one's will, the factors of enlightenment are his spiritual friends; through these he attains perfect awakening.
The various perfections are his companions, and the four means of integration are his courtesans. Chanting and reciting the words of the Dharma serve as his music;
the dhāraṇīs are his gardens, and the untainted dharmas are the trees of his grove.
The flowers of the pure and wondrous awakening-mind, The fruit of liberation and wisdom, The bathing pool of the eight liberations,
filled with the limpid waters of meditative concentration, Spread with the blossoms of the seven purities— In this bath,
the stainless person rides the elephant and horse of the five supernormal powers, With the Great Vehicle as their chariot, And the single mind as their driver.
Wandering upon the Eightfold Path, adorned with the marks that grace the countenance;
Adorned with the secondary signs that beautify the form, having shame and dread as their noble raiment, And the profound mind as their flower garland;
possessing the wealth of the seven treasures, Which increase through instruction, practicing according to what has been taught, And dedicating [the merit] for the sake of great benefit.
The four dhyānas serve as his seat, born from a pure livelihood; Abundant learning increases wisdom, serving as the sound of his self-awakening;
The food is the Dharma of ambrosia, and the flavor of liberation is his drink;
A purified mind serves as his bath, and the precepts serve as his unguent; Thus he utterly destroys the thieves of the afflictions.

Valiant and invincible, he has subdued the four kinds of Māras; Raising the banner of victory at the site of enlightenment, though he knows there is neither arising nor ceasing, He manifests birth for the sake of others, appearing in all lands like the sun that nothing can obscure.
Thus he makes offerings to the immeasurable billions of Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions.
Regarding all Buddhas and one’s own self, there is no thought of discrimination.
Although they know that the Buddha-lands and sentient beings are empty, they constantly cultivate pure lands to teach and transform all classes of living beings.
As for the forms, voices, and dignified deportment of all such sentient beings, the Bodhisattva possesses the power of fearlessness.
At one time they can manifest everything, perceiving all the works of Māra;
yet by means of their wisdom of skillful means, they demonstrate compliance with those ways, manifesting according to their will.
They may manifest old age, sickness, and death to bring all sentient beings to maturity; understanding that these are like illusions and transformations, they penetrate them all without obstruction.
Sometimes he manifests the conflagration at the end of a kalpa, where heaven and earth are all ablaze; illuminating those who harbor notions of permanence so that they may know impermanence.
Countless billions of sentient beings come together to invite the Bodhisattva, arriving at their homes all at once;
he transforms them, causing them to turn toward the Buddha-way, as well as the scriptures, incantations, and arts.
They fully manifest all manner of crafts and arts to benefit all living beings;
among all the worldly paths and dharmas, they renounce the householder’s life. By this means, they resolve the delusions of others so that they do not fall into false views.
Sometimes they become the sun or moon, or gods, or Brahmā, the lord of the world.
At times they become earth or water, and at others they become wind or fire;
when epidemics appear in the kalpa, they manifest as various medicinal herbs, so that whoever consumes them is cured of illness and the many poisons are eliminated.
When famine prevails in the kalpa, they manifest in bodily form as food and drink, first rescuing those from hunger and thirst.

Yet they instruct others with the Dharma; during kalpas of war and weapons, they give rise to compassion for them and transform those sentient beings, causing them to abide in the ground of non-contention.
If there are great battles, they stand amidst them with impartial power; the Bodhisattva manifests majestic might to subdue them and bring about peace and harmony.
In all lands throughout the universe, wherever there are places of hell,
he immediately goes there to diligently rescue them from their suffering. In all lands throughout the universe, wherever animals devour one another,
he manifests birth among them to bring them benefit and show them how to experience the five desires.
They manifest the practice of dhyāna once again, causing the minds of Māras to become confused and agitated so that they cannot find an opportunity.
For a lotus to grow amidst fire is called rare; likewise, to practice dhyāna while remaining in the realm of desire is equally rare.
Sometimes they manifest as courtesans to attract those who are lustful.
First they are enticed with the hook of desire, and later they are led into the Buddha’s wisdom.
Sometimes acting as leaders of towns, or as guides for merchants, or as royal preceptors and great ministers, they benefit and assist all sentient beings.
To those who are poor and destitute, they manifest as inexhaustible treasuries, using this means to exhort and lead them.
To cause them to resolve upon Bodhicitta, for those whose minds are arrogant, he manifests as a mighty wrestler to subdue all haughtiness and establish them in the Unsurpassed Way.
For those who are terrified, he stands before them to offer comfort; first bestowing fearlessness, he subsequently causes them to resolve upon the Bodhi-mind.
Sometimes he manifests as one free from lust, acting as a seer with the five supernatural powers;
he guides all sentient beings, causing them to abide in precepts, patience, and compassion. Seeing those who require service, he manifests as their servant;
having first pleased their minds, he then inspires them with the mind of the Way, according to whatever they may need.

They enter the path of the Buddhas through the power of skillful means, Able to provide for all in such a way that the Way is immeasurable, And their practice has no limit. Their wisdom is boundless as they deliver countless multitudes;
Even if all the Buddhas were to do so for countless billions of eons, [they could not exhaust its measure].
Even if one were to praise his virtues, they could not be fully exhausted.
Who, upon hearing such a Dharma as this, would not resolve to attain Bodhicitta—except for those unworthy persons who are ignorant, deluded, and lacking wisdom?
*The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Nine*
The Chapter on Entering the Dharma-Gate of Non-Duality.
At that time, Vimalakīrti addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: "Virtuous ones, how does a bodhisattva enter the dharma-gate of non-duality?
Each of you should speak according to what you find appropriate."
In the assembly was a bodhisattva named Dharmavasu who declared: "O virtuous ones, arising and ceasing constitute duality.

Since phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, they are now without cessation. To attain this patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is to enter the gate of non-dual dharmas."
The Bodhisattva Guṇapāla said: "Self and what belongs to self constitute duality. Because there is a self, there is what belongs to self;
if there were no self, there would be nothing belonging to self. This is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Animiṣa said: “To accept and not to accept are two. If one does not accept any phenomenon, it cannot be apprehended.
Because it cannot be apprehended, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing, neither action nor activity. This is the entrance into the dharma-gate of non-duality.”
The Bodhisattva Śīrṣabhadra said: "Defilement and purity are two. To see the true nature of defilement is to find no characteristic of purity;
this accords with the mark of cessation. This is the entrance into the dharma-gate of non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Sunakṣatra said: "This movement and this thought constitute duality. When there is no movement, there is no thought;
where there is no thought, there is no discrimination. One who penetrates this enters the gate of non-dual dharmas."
The Bodhisattva Fine Eyes said: "The single characteristic and the absence of characteristics constitute duality.

If one knows that the single characteristic is itself the absence of characteristics, and does not even grasp at the absence of characteristics, thereby entering into equanimity—this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Subāhu said: "The mind of a bodhisattva and the mind of a śrāvaka constitute duality.
One who contemplates the nature of the mind as empty and like an illusion has neither the mind of a bodhisattva nor the mind of a śrāvaka. This is the entrance into the gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Puṣya said: "Good and not-good constitute duality. If one does not give rise to good or not-good, one enters into non-arising."
"To penetrate by means of their mutual interfacing is to enter the dharma-gate of non-duality.
Lion Bodhisattva said: "Offense and merit constitute a duality. If one penetrates the nature of offense, it is no different from merit."
To decisively comprehend these characteristics with vajra-wisdom—that there is neither bondage nor liberation—is the entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhamati said: "The tainted and the untainted constitute a duality. If one attains the equality of all dharmas, then..."
Not giving rise to the notion of outflows, nor the notion of being without outflows; not clinging to signs, nor dwelling in signlessness—this is the entrance into the dharma-gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati said: "The conditioned and the unconditioned constitute a duality. If one departs from all numerical reckonings, then the mind..."
"Like space; because one who possesses pure wisdom is without obstruction, this is called entering the gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa said: "The mundane and the supramundane constitute duality. The empty nature of the mundane is itself the supramundane.
Within it, there is no entering and no exiting, no overflowing and no dispersing. This is called entering [the gate of non-duality]."

Regarding the Dharma-gate of Non-duality, the Bodhisattva Good Intention said: "Birth-and-death and nirvana constitute duality. If one perceives the nature of birth-and-death, then there is no birth-and-death;
there is neither bondage nor liberation, neither arising nor ceasing. To understand it in this way is to enter non-duality."

Second, the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva Pratyakṣadarśin (Manifest Vision) states: "Exhaustion and non-exhaustion constitute duality. Whether a phenomenon is ultimately exhausted or not exhausted, it possesses the characteristic of inexhaustibility.
This characteristic of inexhaustibility is itself emptiness; in emptiness, there is neither exhaustion nor non-exhaustion."
"Characteristics. Entering in this manner is the entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Universal Protector said: "Self and non-self constitute a duality. Since even 'self' cannot be apprehended, how could 'non-self' be apprehended?
One who perceives the true nature of self no longer gives rise to duality; this is the entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Vidyuddeva said: "To distinguish between clarity and ignorance is duality. The true nature of ignorance is itself clarity;
yet even this clarity cannot be grasped. To be free from all numerical categories and to abide in equanimity where there is no duality—this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."

The Bodhisattva Priyadarśana said: "Form and the emptiness of form constitute two. Form itself is emptiness; it is not that form ceases to exist for there to be emptiness, but rather the very nature of form is itself empty.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness: consciousness and the emptiness of consciousness constitute two; consciousness itself is emptiness."
It is not that consciousness ceases to be empty; rather, the very nature of consciousness is itself empty. To penetrate and realize this within it is to enter the gate of the non-dual dharma.
The Bodhisattva Vimalaprabha said:
"The four great elements and the element of space are distinct; these constitute duality. The very nature of the four great elements is itself [the element of space]."
The nature of emptiness: just as the past and future limits are empty, so too is the middle limit empty.
One who can thus know all natures has entered the gateway to the non-dual dharma.

The Bodhisattva Subhamati said: "The eye and forms constitute a duality. If one knows the nature of the eye such that it is neither greedy for, nor angry toward, nor deluded by forms, this is called tranquility.
Likewise, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena constitute dualities.
If one knows the nature of the mind such that it is neither greedy for, nor angry toward, nor deluded by mental phenomena, this is called tranquility."
To extinguish [them] and dwell therein—this is the entrance into the gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said: "Giving and dedicating it toward omniscience are two. The nature of giving is itself the nature of dedication toward omniscience.
It is the same for ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration."
To regard wisdom and its dedication toward omniscience as two is dualistic. The very nature of wisdom is itself the nature of dedication toward omniscience.
To enter into the single characteristic within this is to enter the gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Gambhīraprajñā said: "To regard emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as two is dualistic. Emptiness is itself signlessness;
signlessness is itself wishlessness. If emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are thus one, then there is no mind, thought, or consciousness.
That which is a single gate of liberation is itself the three gates of liberation—this is entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Silent Root said: "The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha constitute duality. The Buddha is itself the Dharma; the Dharma is itself the Sangha.
These Three Jewels all possess the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and are equal to empty space. All dharmas are likewise so.
One who can practice in accordance with this enters the gate of non-dual dharmas."
The Bodhisattva Unobstructed Mind said: "The body and the extinction of the body constitute two. The body is itself the extinction of the body. Why is this?
For one who perceives the true reality of the body does not give rise to the view of a body, nor the view of the extinction of a body.
Body and the extinction of the body are non-dual and without distinction. To be neither startled nor afraid within this is to enter the non-dual."
Second, regarding the Dharma-gate:
The Bodhisattva Shangshan said, "The goodness of body, speech, and mind constitutes two. These three karmas are all characterized by non-action.

The characteristic of non-action of the body is identical to the characteristic of non-action of speech; the characteristic of non-action of speech is identical to the characteristic of non-action of the mind."
These three karmas have the characteristic of non-action; this is the characteristic of non-action of all dharmas.
One who can thus accord with the wisdom of non-action enters the gate of the non-dual dharma.
The Bodhisattva Puṇyakṣetra said: "Meritorious action, non-meritorious action, and immovable action constitute duality.
The true nature of these three types of action is emptiness. In emptiness, there is no meritorious action, no non-meritorious action, and no immovable action.
To not give rise to [the conceptualization of] these three types of action is to enter the gate of non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Flower Adornment said: "To give rise to duality from me constitutes duality. One who perceives my true reality does not give rise to dualistic dharmas.
If one does not abide in dualistic dharmas, then there is no consciousness. That which has nothing to be cognized is the entrance into the gate of non-dual dharmas."
The Bodhisattva Guṇagañja said: "To have the mark of attainment is duality. If there is nothing attained, then there is neither grasping nor rejecting.
That which is without grasping or rejecting is the entrance into the gateway of non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Candrottara said: "Darkness and light constitute a duality. Where there is neither darkness nor light, there is no duality. Why is this?
It is because, as in the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, there is neither darkness nor light; such is the characteristic of all phenomena."
It is also like this. Regarding those who enter into equality therein:
the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta said, "To delight in nirvāṇa and not to delight in the world constitutes duality.
If one does not delight in nirvāṇa and does not loathe the world, then there is no duality. Why is this? If there were bondage, then..."
There is liberation. If there were originally no bondage, who would seek liberation? Where there is neither bondage nor liberation, there is neither delight nor aversion;
this is entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Maṇicūḍarāja said: "The right path and the wrong path constitute a duality.
One who abides in the right path does not discriminate between what is wrong and what is right. To be free from these two is to enter the gate of non-dual dharmas."
The Bodhisattva Ratisatya said: "Reality and unreality constitute a duality. One who perceives reality does not even perceive reality, let alone unreality.
Why is this? It is not that which is seen by the fleshly eye; it is only the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) that can see it.
Yet this wisdom-eye neither sees nor does not see. This is entry into the gate of non-duality."
When these bodhisattvas had each finished speaking, they asked Mañjuśrī,
"What is the bodhisattva’s entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality?
Mañjuśrī replied, "According to my understanding, regarding all dharmas, there is no speech and no discourse."
To manifest non-consciousness and to be free from all questioning and answering—this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti: "We have each spoken for ourselves; now, O Benevolent One, you should speak:
what is the Bodhisattva’s entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality?"
At that time, Vimalakīrti remained silent and spoke no word. Mañjuśrī praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
Even the absence of all written characters and speech is the true entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."

When this "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-Gate of Non-Duality" was being expounded, five thousand bodhisattvas within this assembly all entered the dharma-gate of non-duality and attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

In the tenth fascicle of the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, "The Chapter on the Buddha of Fragrant Accumulation," Śāriputra then thought to himself: "The time for the midday meal is approaching; where will these bodhisattvas eat?"
At that time, Vimalakīrti, knowing his thoughts, said to him: "The Buddha has taught the eight liberations;
you, O noble one, should practice them. How can you listen to the Dharma while occupied with the desire for food? If you must eat, wait but a moment."
"I shall cause you to obtain food such as you have never experienced before.

At that time, Vimalakīrti entered into samādhi and, by means of his supernatural powers, revealed to the great assembly the region above, beyond Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers.
There was a land named Saugandhika, where the Buddha was named Gandhottama; he is currently residing there. The fragrance of that land, compared to...
Among the fragrances of gods and humans in the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, this is the most supreme.
