In that land, there is no mention of the names of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; there are only pure assemblies of great bodhisattvas. The Buddha preaches the Dharma for them.
Throughout that realm, all things are made of fragrance: there are pavilions of fragrance, walkways of fragrant ground, and even gardens and groves are likewise composed of fragrance.
Fragrance. The fragrance of that food circulated throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions.

At that time, while that Buddha was sitting together with the bodhisattvas to partake of the meal, there were sons of gods, all named Gandhavimāna (Fragrance-Adorned), who had all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and were making offerings to that Buddha and the bodhisattvas. These...
The great assembly all witnessed this with their own eyes. Then Vimalakīrti asked the bodhisattvas, "Virtuous ones, who among you can bring back the food from that Buddha?
Due to the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī, they all remained silent.
Vimalakīrti said, "O virtuous one, this great assembly might find this shameful. Mañjuśrī replied, "As the Buddha has said, do not despise those who have not yet studied.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti, without rising from his seat, manifested before the assembly a bodhisattva of exquisite marks and signs, radiant and of surpassing majesty, who eclipsed the entire gathering.
And he addressed him, saying: "Go to the region above, passing through as many Buddha-fields as there are sands in forty-two Ganges Rivers.
There is a land named Saṃghagandha; the Buddha there is named Gandhottama. He is currently sitting together with various bodhisattvas, partaking of a meal.
Go there and speak these words on my behalf: 'Vimalakīrti bows his head at the feet of the World-Honored One.'"
I pay my respects with boundless reverence. I inquire after your well-being and daily life. I hope you suffer but slight illness and but slight distress, and that your strength remains secure.

I pray that I may receive the remnants of the World-Honored One’s meal; I shall perform the work of a Buddha within this Sahā world, so that those who delight in inferior teachings may attain the Great Way, and so that the fame of the Tathāgata may be heard everywhere, transforming beings at that time.
The Bodhisattva immediately ascended to the upper regions before the assembly. The entire multitude saw him go to the world-system of Gandhavatī, where he prostrated at the feet of that Buddha.
Furthermore, they heard him say: "Vimalakīrti bows his head at the feet of the World-Honored One.
He pays infinite respects and inquires after your well-being, asking whether you have little illness and little affliction, and whether your strength and vigor are secure. He then made this request:

Having obtained the remains of the World-Honored One’s meal, he desired to perform buddha-work within the Sahā world so that those who delight in inferior dharmas might attain the Great Way, and so that the fame of the Tathāgata might be heard everywhere.
When those great beings saw this transformed bodhisattva, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, asking, "From where has this superior person come?"
"Come! Where is this Sahā world located? Why is it called 'those who delight in inferior teachings'?
He asked the Buddha, who replied to him: "Below here, past as many buddha-fields as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sahā.
The Buddha there is titled Śākyamuni, and he currently resides within the five [corruptions]."
In this world of turbid evil, for the sake of sentient beings who delight in inferior teachings, I have expounded the Way and its doctrines.
There is a bodhisattva there named Vimalakīrti, who dwells in the inconceivable liberation and preaches the Dharma for the sake of all bodhisattvas;
therefore, he has sent a transformation body here to proclaim my name and to praise this land, so as to cause those bodhisattvas to increase their merit and virtue.
That bodhisattva asked, "What kind of person is it that can produce such emanations, possessing such power of virtue, fearlessness, and supernormal powers as these?
The Buddha said, "They are exceedingly great; they dispatch emanations throughout all the ten directions to perform the work of a Buddha."
To benefit sentient beings, the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa then took a bowl of fragrant incense and filled it with fragrant food, giving it to the emanated bodhisattva.
At that time, those nine million bodhisattvas spoke with one voice:
"We wish to go to the Sahā world to make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, and we also wish to see Vimalakīrti and the others."
The Buddha said to the assembly of bodhisattvas, "You may go, but restrain your bodily fragrance so as not to cause those sentient beings to give rise to thoughts of delusion or attachment.
Furthermore, you must relinquish your original forms so as not to cause those in that land who seek to become bodhisattvas [to be distracted]."
And you should feel self-reproach and shame. Furthermore, regarding that [land], do not harbor thoughts of contempt or create obstacles in your mind.

Why is this? All lands in the ten directions are like empty space; moreover, because the Buddhas wish to transform those who delight in inferior teachings, they do not fully manifest their pure lands. At that time, the transformed Bodhisattva, having received the bowl...

Having partaken of the meal, together with those nine million bodhisattvas, they suddenly vanished from that world through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha and the strength of Vimalakīrti. In an instant, they arrived at the house of Vimalakīrti.
At that time, Vimalakīrti immediately manifested nine million lion-thrones, as magnificent and well-adorned as before. All...
The bodhisattvas all sat upon them. Then the manifested bodhisattva took a bowl filled with fragrant food and gave it to Vimalakīrti.
The fragrance of the food permeated the city of Vaiśālī as well as the trichiliocosm.
At that time, the brahmins, householders, and others in Vaiśālī, having smelled this fragrance, felt their bodies and minds become refreshed and joyful, and they marveled at it.
Once, the elder Candracchattra, accompanied by eighty-four thousand people, entered the house of Vimalakīrti.
Seeing that his chamber was filled with a great multitude of bodhisattvas and that the lion thrones were high, broad, and magnificently adorned, he was filled with great joy.
He prostrated before the bodhisattvas and the great disciples, then withdrew to stand to one side. All...
The earth spirits, the spirits of space, and the various devas of the desire and form realms, having smelled this fragrance, also all came into Vimalakīrti’s house.
Then Vimalakīrti spoke to Śāriputra and the other great śrāvakas:
"Virtuous one, you may eat this meal of the Tathāgata’s ambrosial flavor, which is permeated by great compassion.

Do not eat it with a limited mind, lest it remain undigested. A transformed bodhisattva said, "Do not attempt to measure this with the small virtues and small wisdom of a śrāvaka, thinking that this food is insufficient for each member of this great assembly to eat."
The Tathāgata possesses immeasurable merit and wisdom; while the four oceans may run dry, this food is inexhaustible.
Even if all people were to eat it in morsels as large as Mount Sumeru, they could not finish it even in an eon. Why is this?
It is because it is the food of one who is fully endowed with the merits of inexhaustible morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
It could not be exhausted. Thereupon, the food in the bowl satisfied the entire assembly, yet it was still not finished.
Those bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, and humans who ate this food felt their bodies at ease and happy, just like the bodhisattvas in the land of Sarva-sukha-vyūha.
Furthermore, a wondrous fragrance issued from every one of their pores.
It was also like the fragrance of the trees in the land of Sarvagandhasugandhā. At that time, Vimalakīrti asked the bodhisattvas from the Fragrant Land:
"How does the Tathāgata Sugandhakūṭa teach the Dharma? Those bodhisattvas replied: "In our land, the Tathāgata..."
There is no teaching by means of written words; rather, it causes all devas and humans to enter into the practice of the precepts through various fragrances.
Each bodhisattva sits beneath a fragrant tree, and upon smelling this wondrous fragrance, they immediately attain the Samādhi of the Treasury of All Virtues.
Those who attain this samādhi are fully endowed with all the merits of a bodhisattva.
The bodhisattvas there asked Vimalakīrti, "How does the World-Honored One Śākyamuni teach the Dharma now?
Vimalakīrti replied, "The sentient beings of this land are stubborn and difficult to transform; therefore, the Buddha speaks words of firm severity for their sake."
He subdues them by saying: "This is hell; this is the animal realm; this is the realm of hungry ghosts; these are the states of adversity;
these are the birthplaces of fools; this is misconduct of the body; this is the retribution for misconduct of the body; this is misconduct of speech."
This is the retribution for misconduct of speech. This is misconduct of mind. This is the retribution for misconduct of mind.

This is killing. This is the retribution for killing. This is taking what is not given. This is the retribution for taking what is not given. This is sexual misconduct. This is the retribution for sexual misconduct.
This is false speech. This is the retribution for false speech. This is divisive speech. This is the retribution for divisive speech. This is harsh speech.
This is the retribution for harsh speech; this is frivolous speech; this is the retribution for frivolous speech; this is greed and envy; this is the retribution for greed and envy;
this is anger and vexation; this is the retribution for anger and vexation; this is wrong view; this is the retribution for wrong view;
this is stinginess; this is the retribution for stinginess; this is the violation of precepts; this is the retribution for violating precepts; this is malice. This is malice.
Retribution; this is laziness, this is the retribution for laziness; this is distraction, this is the retribution for distraction;
this is delusion, this is the retribution for delusion; this is the precept, this is the upholding of the precept, this is the violation of the precept;
this is what should be done, this is what should not be done; this is an obstacle, this is not an obstacle; this is the incurrence of fault, this is the departure from fault; this is purity.
It is defiled; it is with outflows (*sāsrava*); it is without outflows (*anāsrava*). It is the false path; it is the true path.
It is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). It is the mundane world (*loka*); it is nirvāṇa.

Because the minds of those difficult to transform are like monkeys, one must subdue them by means of various kinds of dharmas before they can be tamed. It is, for example, like an elephant or a horse that is obstinate and unruly.
They were unruly; they were subjected to various forms of torment until it pierced to the very bone before they were finally subdued.
Such are these stubborn and difficult-to-transform sentient beings; therefore, only through words of the utmost severity can they be brought into the discipline.
When those bodhisattvas heard this teaching, they all said, "It is unprecedented! It is as the World-Honored One Śākyamuni..."
The Buddha, concealing his immeasurable power of mastery, delivers sentient beings by means of the Dharma that accords with their poverty.
These bodhisattvas likewise endure toil and humility, and through immeasurable great compassion, they are born in this buddha-field.
Vimalakīrti said: "The great compassion of the bodhisattvas in this land toward all sentient beings is firm and steadfast; it is indeed true."

As it has been said: nevertheless, the benefit for sentient beings achieved in a single lifetime here exceeds that which would be attained by practicing in those other lands for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Why is this? Because this Sahā world possesses ten virtuous dharmas that do not exist in other pure lands.
What are these ten? First, gathering in the poor through generosity; second, through pure ethical discipline...

They gather in those who violate the precepts; they gather in those who harbor anger through patience; they gather in those who are indolent through diligence; they gather in those with distracted minds through meditative concentration;
and they gather in those who are deluded through wisdom. They preach the Dharma for removing obstacles to deliver those in the eight difficult conditions.
They deliver those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle by means of the Mahāyāna. They rescue those who lack virtue by means of all roots of goodness. Always, with...
The four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) for maturing sentient beings—these constitute the ten. That bodhisattva asked:
"By accomplishing how many dharmas does a bodhisattva, while in this world, remain free from wounds and sores and be born in a pure land? Vimalakīrti replied:
"A bodhisattva who accomplishes eight dharmas remains free from wounds and sores while in this world and is born in a pure land. What are they?"
These constitute eight [qualities]. They benefit sentient beings without expecting a reward; they undergo all manner of suffering and affliction on behalf of all sentient beings;
they dedicate all the merit they perform entirely to them; they regard all sentient beings with an impartial mind; and they are humble and free from obstruction.
Regarding all bodhisattvas, one should view them as Buddhas. When hearing sutras not previously heard, one should do so without doubt.
One should not conflict with the śrāvakas; one should not envy the offerings given to others nor exalt one's own gain, but rather subdue the mind therein.
One should constantly examine one's own faults and never speak of the shortcomings of others, always seeking [the Dharma] with a single-minded focus.
These are the eight dharmas. When Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī preached these teachings in the midst of the great assembly,
hundreds of thousands of devas and humans all resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
and ten thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Volume Eleven:
Chapter on the Conduct of Bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Buddha was preaching the Dharma in the Āmra Grove. Suddenly, that ground became vast, expansive, and magnificently adorned.
The entire assembly was transformed into the color of gold. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions has this auspicious omen appeared?
Suddenly, this place has become vast and magnificent, and the entire assembly has been turned into the color of gold.
The Buddha told Ānanda, “This is because Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī, together with the great [bodhisattvas]...”
The assembly, surrounding him with reverence, had resolved to come; therefore, he first manifested this auspicious omen.
Then, Vimalakīrti said to Mañjuśrī, “We should go together to see the Buddha and pay our respects and make offerings along with the bodhisattvas.
Mañjuśrī replied, “Excellent! Let us go; now is precisely the right time. Thereupon, Vimalakīrti...
By means of his supernormal power, he took the great assembly along with their lion thrones, placed them upon his right palm, and proceeded to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he set them down on the ground, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and stood to one side with palms joined in single-minded devotion.
Thereupon, all those bodhisattvas likewise rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and also circumambulated him seven times.
They stood to one side. The great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Great Kings, and others likewise all vacated their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
Then the World-Honored One, having comforted the bodhisattvas according to the Dharma, bade each of them return to their seats;
they all complied with his instruction. Once the assembly was seated, the Buddha spoke to Śāriputra:
“Ānanda, do you see the deeds performed by the sovereign spiritual power of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas?
“Indeed, I see them, World-Honored One. “What do you think? Ānanda, how do you perceive their actions? “They are inconceivable, World-Honored One;
they cannot be conceived by the mind, nor can they be measured by the intellect. At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, as for what has now been heard...”
"An incense such as this has never existed since ancient times. What kind of incense is this? The Buddha told Ānanda, "This is the fragrance from the pores of that bodhisattva.
Thereupon, Śāriputra said to Ānanda, "Fragrance like this also issues from our own pores.
Ānanda asked, "From where does this come? He replied, "It comes from the elder Vimalakīrti and his assembly."
In the Land of Fragrance, those who take the food remaining from the Buddha and eat it in their homes find that all their pores are fragrant in this very way.
Ānanda asked Vimalakīrti, "How long will this fragrance remain? Vimalakīrti replied, "It will remain until this food is digested.
Ānanda asked, "How long will it take for this food to be digested? He replied, "The power of this food lasts for seven [kalpas]."

After one day, it will then be digested. Furthermore, Ānanda, if a śrāvaka who has not yet entered the state of certainty eats this food, he shall enter that state of certainty, and only then will it be digested.
If one who has already entered the state of certainty eats this food, [it will be digested immediately].
It is digested only after one attains liberation of mind. If one has not yet resolved upon the Great Vehicle, the food will be digested once that resolve is generated.
For those who have already resolved upon it, the food is digested only after they attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
For those who have already attained the patience of non-arising, the food is digested only upon reaching the stage of being "one birth away from Buddhahood" (*ekajātipratibaddha*). Then...
Then it was digested. It is like a medicine called "Supreme Flavor" (*uttaravara*); whoever consumes it has all the poisons in their body eliminated, and only then is it digested.
This rice is just so: it eliminates the poisons of all afflictions (*kleśa*), and only then is it digested.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "It is unprecedented! World-Honored One, such fragrant rice is able to..."
[They] perform the work of a Buddha. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Ānanda.
There are some buddha-fields where the work of a Buddha is performed by the Buddha’s radiance; some where it is performed by various bodhisattvas;
some where it is performed by beings emanated by the Buddha; some where it is performed by the Bodhi tree; and some where it is performed by the Buddha..."
They perform the work of a Buddha through robes and bedding. Some perform the work of a Buddha through food and drink (the faculty of the tongue serving as the conduit).

Some perform the work of a Buddha through gardens, groves, and palatial towers (the faculty of the eye serving as the conduit). Some perform the work of a Buddha through the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics.
Some perform the work of a Buddha through the Buddha-body (manifesting the entire body). Some perform the work of a Buddha through empty space.
They perform the work of a Buddha (extinguishing all forms and images). Sentient beings, by means of these conditions, are able to enter into the practice of the Vinaya.
There are those who perform the work of a Buddha using such metaphors as a dream, an illusion, a reflection, an image in a mirror, the moon in water, and a mirage in the heat.
There are those who perform the work of a Buddha through sounds, speech, and written words;

yet there are also pure buddha-fields that are silent, where there is no speaking and no discourse, no demonstrating and no cognition, and no action or conditioning, and therein they perform the work of a Buddha.
Thus it is, Ānanda. In all the majestic deportment and movements of the Buddhas, and in all their actions, there is nothing that is not the work of a Buddha.
Ānanda, there are these four māras and eighty-four thousand gateways of affliction, yet sentient beings—
They become weary of it. Yet, the Buddhas perform their Buddha-works precisely by means of this very dharma; this is called "entering the gateway to all Buddha-dharmas.

When a bodhisattva enters this gateway, if they see any pure and beautiful buddha-fields, they do not feel joy, nor do they crave them or become arrogant. If they see any impure buddha-fields, they do not...
Do not let this cause you distress. Be neither hindered nor discouraged; rather, toward all Buddhas, give rise to a pure mind of joy and reverence—this has never been before.

The merits of all Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are equal; it is only for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings that they manifest different Buddha-lands. Ānanda, as for the various Buddha-lands you see, whether their grounds...

They are manifold, yet empty space is not manifold. In this same way, while the physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) of the Buddhas appear to be manifold, their unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇajñāna*) is not manifold.

Ānanda, the physical bodies, majestic marks, lineage, ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of the Buddhas—[are likewise manifold].

The Dharma, great kindness and great compassion, the conduct of his majestic demeanor, as well as his lifespan, his preaching of the Dharma for the sake of transforming beings, his bringing of sentient beings to maturity, his purification of Buddha-lands, and his possession of all Buddha-dharmas—all these are entirely equal.
For this reason, he is named Samyaksaṃbuddha; he is named Tathāgata; he is named Buddha. A.
Difficult. If I were to explain the meaning of these three phrases in detail, you could not fully grasp them even with a lifespan of an eon.

Even if the beings filling a trichiliocosm were all like Ānanda, foremost in much-hearing, having attained mindfulness and dhāraṇī, these people together could not grasp them even with a lifespan of an eon. Just as...
"Ānanda, the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas is without limit;
their wisdom and eloquence are inconceivable. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "From this day forward..."
"I did not dare to claim for myself that I was one of great learning. The Buddha told Ānanda, "Do not give rise to thoughts of retreat.
Why is this? I have said that among the śrāvakas, you are the most learned; I did not mean this in comparison to the bodhisattvas. Cease now, Ānanda!
One who possesses wisdom should not attempt to measure the bodhisattvas, for they are like all the oceans."
"A deep abyss may still be measured, but the bodhisattva’s meditative concentration, wisdom, dhāraṇīs, eloquence,
and all their merits are immeasurable. Ānanda, setting aside for a moment the conduct of the bodhisattvas,
even all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, in a hundred [eons]..."
"Even with all one's power and through transformations spanning a thousand kalpas, one could not have produced such a thing.

At that time, the bodhisattvas who had come from the World of Universal Fragrance joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, when we first saw this land, we conceived thoughts of inferiority.
We now repent and reproach ourselves, having abandoned and left behind such a mind. Why is this? Because the skillful means of the Buddhas are [inconceivable]...'"
It is inconceivable. For the sake of delivering sentient beings, he manifests various Buddha-lands according to what is appropriate for each.
"Indeed, World-Honored One, we pray that you will grant us a brief teaching so that, upon returning to our own lands, we may remain mindful of the Tathāgata. The Buddha told the bodhisattvas:
"There is a dharma-gate of liberation called 'Exhaustion and Non-exhaustion. You should study it. What is meant by 'exhaustion'? It is said:
Regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*): what is meant by "inexhaustible"? It refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). As for a bodhisattva:

they do not exhaust conditioned phenomena (being free from the hindrance of ordinary beings), yet they do not dwell in unconditioned phenomena (being free from the hindrance of the two vehicles). What is meant by "not exhausting conditioned phenomena" (the opening phrase)?

It means not being separated from great kindness (*maitrī*), not abandoning great compassion (*karuṇā*), deeply generating the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) without neglecting it, and teaching and transforming sentient beings without ever ceasing.
Free from weariness, they constantly mindfully practice the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). They protect and uphold the true Dharma, not begrudging even their own bodies or lives.
They plant all manner of roots of goodness without ever feeling fatigue or weariness. Their resolve always dwells in peace as they employ skillful means for dedication.
They seek the Dharma without slackening and preach it without stinginess. Diligently making offerings to all Buddhas, they enter the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) without any fear.
Regarding all honors and insults, his mind is free from sorrow or joy; he does not slight those who have not yet studied, but respects those who have studied as if they were Buddhas;
toward those fallen into afflictions, he causes them to give rise to right mindfulness; he does not regard the pleasure of seclusion as supreme, nor does he cling to his own pleasure.

One rejoices in those pleasures found within the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) as one would perceive them as being in hell. One regards the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) as a pleasure grove.
Upon seeing those who come seeking [help], one regards them as virtuous teachers. Regarding the relinquishing of all possessions, one maintains the perception of attaining omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Upon seeing those who violate the precepts, one gives rise to the thought of rescuing and protecting them. One regards the perfections (*pāramitā*) as one's parents. The Path...
Regarding the dharmas of this stage, one should conceive of them as being like one's own retinue.

One should cultivate roots of goodness without limit, using the various adornments of pure lands to perfect one’s own Buddha-field. Practicing boundless generosity, one is endowed with the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha.
Eliminating all evils, one purifies body, speech, and mind; thus, throughout countless kalpas of birth and death, the mind remains courageous. Upon hearing...
The Buddha possesses immeasurable virtues; he is resolute and never weary. With the sword of wisdom, he slays the thieves of affliction and emerges from the aggregates and realms.
Carrying the burden of sentient beings upon his shoulders, he brings them eternal liberation.

Through great diligence, he subdues the armies of Māra and constantly seeks the wisdom of the non-conceptual true mark (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*). He practices few desires and contentment, yet does not abandon worldly dharmas (whereby all in the world say, "He is just like me").

Practicing such dharmas as these is called the Bodhisattva’s non-exhaustion of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). What is meant by the Bodhisattva’s non-abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? It means practicing and studying emptiness, yet not [clinging to it].
Taking emptiness as the witness, they practice and study signlessness and wishlessness, yet do not take signlessness and wishlessness as their witness.
They practice and study non-arising, yet do not take non-arising as their witness. They contemplate impermanence, yet do not grow weary of the roots of goodness.
He contemplates the suffering of the world, yet does not loathe birth and death; he contemplates non-self, yet teaches others without weariness;
he contemplates cessation, yet does not enter final cessation; he contemplates detachment, yet cultivates goodness with body and mind.
Contemplating that there is nowhere to which one returns, yet returning to and taking refuge in wholesome dharmas;
contemplating non-arising, yet bearing all beings upon oneself through the dharma of arising; contemplating the outflow-free, yet not severing the various outflows;

contemplating non-action, yet teaching and transforming sentient beings through the dharma of action; contemplating emptiness and nothingness, yet not abandoning great compassion; contemplating the True Dharma...
Abiding [in this state], one does not follow the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). One contemplates that all phenomena are illusory, lacking solidity, lacking a person, lacking a master, and lacking marks.
Yet, while one’s original vows are not yet fulfilled, one does not let merit, meditative concentration, and wisdom go to waste. One cultivates such dharmas as these.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s non-abiding in the unconditioned (the concluding phrase). Furthermore, because he possesses merit and virtue, he does not abide in the unconditioned;

They possess no self-characteristic, no other-characteristic, no non-characteristic, and no grasped characteristic. They do not abide on this shore, nor on the other shore, nor in the middle stream as they transform sentient beings.
They contemplate quiescent extinction, yet do not undergo eternal cessation; they are neither here nor there, and do not rely upon this.
It is not by means of that; it cannot be known by wisdom, nor can it be cognized by consciousness. It is without darkness and without light; without name and without mark;

Patient yet not resentful; neither advancing nor indolent; neither fixed nor distracted; neither wise nor foolish; neither sincere nor deceitful;

Bound by such wisdom as these, they are equal to all sentient beings; they are without discrimination regarding all phenomena. They have neither gain nor loss, neither turbidity nor affliction.

They reach the stage of non-retrogression and accomplish the six perfections. They skillfully discern meanings, accord with the Dharma of Bodhi, and stand at the pinnacle of all sutras.

As taught by all the Buddhas: if one hears such sūtras as these, believes, understands, accepts, maintains, reads, and recites them, and through the power of skillful means, analyzes and explains them for the sake of all sentient beings, manifesting them clearly, it is for the purpose of protecting the Dharma.

Having heard this teaching, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it is unprecedented! As the Buddha has spoken, I shall [act accordingly]..."
May they remain far removed from such evils. May they uphold the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which the Tathāgata has accumulated over countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Furthermore, in future ages, may those sons and daughters of good family who seek the Mahāyāna obtain sūtras such as these in their own hands, and may I grant them the power of mindfulness.

"May they receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and explain it extensively for others. World-Honored One, if in the future final age there are those who can receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and explain it to others, one should know that this is established by the supernatural power of Maitreya."
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Maitreya! It is just as you have spoken; the Buddha rejoices in your joy.

Thereupon, all the bodhisattvas joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying, "We, too, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, shall widely proclaim and disseminate the Dharma of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* throughout the lands of the ten directions. Furthermore, they should...
They shall guide and instruct all who preach the Dharma, enabling them to obtain this sutra. At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, wherever there may be cities, towns, villages, mountain forests, or wildernesses, if this scroll of the sutra exists,"
"To those who read, recite, explain, and comment upon it, I shall lead my retinue of officials to go to their location for the sake of hearing the Dharma;
I shall protect such persons for a radius of one hundred yojanas, ensuring that no one seeking an opportunity to harm them can find an opening."
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda, "Receive and uphold this sutra, and propagate it widely.
Ānanda replied, "Yes, I shall receive and uphold it. However, World-Honored One, what should this sutra be named?
The Buddha said, "Ānanda, this sutra is named 'The Teaching of Vimalakīrti,' and it is also called 'The Dharma-Door of Inconceivable Liberation.'"

Thus it was received and upheld. When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the elder Vimalakīrti, Mañjuśrī, Śāriputra, Ānanda, and the entire assembly—including devas, humans, asuras, and all others—having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced;
they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
